one_line_idea: The last transformer layer of contrastively pretrained vision-language models is systematically the worst layer for dense language alignment, because global-pooling pressure concentrates text alignment in summary tokens at the expense of patch tokens.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contrastive image-text pretraining optimizes a global image-level alignment objective, yet open-vocabulary segmentation pipelines routinely extract patch features from the final layer by default.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Patch-to-text alignment quality is non-monotonic across depth and peaks at intermediate layers, with the final layer sacrificing spatially faithful patch semantics to serve the pooled global representation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A per-layer probe of patch-to-text similarity against ground-truth pixel labels will show intermediate layers outperforming the final layer for dense labeling across multiple public contrastive VLMs, and the gap will grow with pretraining scale.
why_important: Nearly all training-free open-vocabulary segmentation methods inherit the final-layer default; if the default is systematically wrong, a large family of methods is leaving accuracy on the table for free.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Layer-wise probing is common for classification features, but a systematic depth-versus-dense-language-alignment characterization across contrastive VLM families, tied to the pooling-pressure mechanism, may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Freeze several public contrastive VLMs, compute patch-text similarity maps from every layer, evaluate each layer as a zero-shot segmenter on one standard semantic segmentation benchmark, and plot dense mIoU versus depth.
main_risk: Layer effects may be confounded with feature norm and anisotropy differences across depth, requiring careful normalization before attributing the effect to alignment rather than scaling artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners assume the final layer is the most semantic layer and therefore the best interface to the text encoder for any granularity of prediction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The final layer is optimized to feed a pooled global embedding, and there is no gradient pressure for individual patch tokens there to remain locally faithful; intermediate layers face no such pressure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One public VLM, one segmentation validation set, sweep all layers as zero-shot dense classifiers in a single inference pass per layer, and check whether the final layer is beaten by any intermediate layer.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary segmentation leaderboards measure mask-proposal quality, not language grounding: swapping the text encoder barely moves scores while swapping the class-agnostic mask generator moves them dramatically.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dominant open-vocabulary segmentation systems decompose into a class-agnostic mask proposal stage and a region-text classification stage, and reported gains are usually attributed to better vision-language alignment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Variance in benchmark scores across published systems is dominated by the proposal stage, so cross-system comparisons mostly rank mask generators rather than grounding methods.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A factorial experiment crossing several proposal networks with several region classifiers will attribute the majority of score variance to the proposal factor, and oracle-proposal experiments will compress the gaps between grounding methods substantially.
why_important: If grounding contributions are small relative to proposal contributions, the field's claimed progress on language grounding is partially an artifact of engineering the segmentation stage, and research effort is being misallocated.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Oracle-mask ablations appear in individual papers, but a systematic cross-method variance decomposition separating proposal quality from grounding quality may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a benchmark, cross three public mask proposal models with three public region-text classifiers plus an oracle-mask condition, and run a two-factor analysis of the resulting mIoU matrix.
main_risk: Proposal and classification stages interact (classifiers are tuned to their proposal distribution), so naive component swapping may understate what jointly-trained systems achieve.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community reads open-vocabulary segmentation gains as evidence of better vision-language alignment, treating the mask stage as a solved commodity component.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class-agnostic mask quality varies widely across generators and directly upper-bounds every downstream metric, whereas region classification over a fixed vocabulary is comparatively saturated.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one published open-vocabulary segmenter, replace its proposals with oracle ground-truth masks and separately with a weaker proposal network, and compare the two deltas to the gap between the top published methods.

one_line_idea: Two-stage segment-then-classify pipelines are structurally biased against stuff categories because cropping a region for classification destroys exactly the context that defines stuff.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Region-based open-vocabulary classification typically feeds cropped or masked regions into an image-level VLM, and stuff categories such as ground, wall, or vegetation derive identity partly from spatial context and extent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The crop-and-classify interface causes a systematic thing-versus-stuff performance asymmetry that is a property of the interface, not of the underlying VLM's knowledge.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying open-vocabulary segmentation errors by thing versus stuff will show the two-stage pipelines losing disproportionately on stuff relative to single-stage dense-similarity methods using the same backbone, and context-preserving classification variants will recover a large part of the stuff gap.
why_important: Stuff classes cover most pixels in typical scenes, so an interface-level bias against them caps real-world usefulness of the dominant architecture family regardless of backbone progress.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Thing-stuff gaps are reported descriptively, but attributing the gap causally to the cropping interface via controlled context-preservation interventions may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one benchmark with thing and stuff annotations, compare crop-based, masked-attention-based, and full-image-context region classification over identical proposals and backbones, reporting thing and stuff mIoU separately.
main_risk: Stuff categories also have noisier ground-truth boundaries, so part of any observed gap may reflect annotation ambiguity rather than the classification interface.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Researchers treat region classification as category-neutral and expect scaling the VLM to lift things and stuff equally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A cropped patch of grass, carpet, or asphalt is often visually ambiguous in isolation; the VLM never sees the spatial support that disambiguates it, so no amount of backbone scaling fixes the interface.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Classify ground-truth regions from one scene-parsing validation set through the same VLM twice, once as tight crops and once with full-image context and mask pooling, and compare stuff-class accuracy between the two modes.

one_line_idea: Training-free attention-surgery methods for dense CLIP-style inference gain mostly by spatially denoising features, and simple spatial smoothing of unmodified features recovers much of their improvement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A family of training-free methods modifies the final attention block of contrastive VLMs (for example replacing query-key attention with self-self variants) and reports large zero-shot segmentation gains attributed to better localization.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial fraction of these gains comes from generic spatial regularization of noisy patch maps rather than from genuinely improved patch-to-text alignment.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying plain local smoothing or graph-based label propagation to vanilla patch-text similarity maps will close a large share of the gap to attention-surgery methods, and combining surgery with smoothing will show strongly sub-additive gains.
why_important: Correct attribution matters: if the mechanism is denoising, effort should go into principled spatial priors rather than increasingly exotic attention rewiring, and claimed alignment insights may be overstated.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attention-surgery papers compare against vanilla baselines but may not control for the trivially available smoothing confound in a systematic mechanism study.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On two zero-shot segmentation benchmarks, evaluate vanilla features, vanilla plus smoothing, attention surgery, and surgery plus smoothing over the same backbone and prompts, and measure gain overlap.
main_risk: Different surgery variants may have genuinely different mechanisms, so a single representative method could over- or under-state the family-wide conclusion.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] These modifications are believed to reveal latent dense alignment hidden by an ill-suited final attention pattern, a representational insight rather than a filtering effect.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Self-similarity attention is mathematically close to feature-space non-local smoothing, so the operation may simply be an adaptive denoiser wearing an architectural costume.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one benchmark, four conditions (vanilla, smoothed, surgery, surgery plus smoothed) run in an afternoon; sub-additivity of the last condition is the key readout.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary segmenters are closed-vocabulary in disguise: per-class dense accuracy is largely predictable from the class name's frequency in web caption corpora.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary segmentation is marketed as handling arbitrary category names, yet the underlying VLMs are trained on web image-text pairs whose caption vocabulary is heavily skewed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-class IoU of open-vocabulary segmenters is strongly predicted by caption-corpus name frequency after controlling for visual difficulty, implying the open vocabulary is effectively bounded by caption statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Regressing per-class IoU on log name-frequency in a public caption corpus will show a strong positive relationship that persists after controlling for class pixel area, boundary complexity, and closed-set difficulty measured by a supervised model.
why_important: If capability is caption-frequency-bounded, claims of open-vocabulary generalization to rare domains such as industrial or scientific imagery are unsupported, and users need frequency-aware reliability estimates.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frequency effects are documented for zero-shot classification, but a dense-prediction version with visual-difficulty controls and a practical per-class reliability predictor may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute name frequencies from one public caption corpus, evaluate one open-vocabulary segmenter per-class on a many-category benchmark, and fit a regression with visual-difficulty covariates from a fully supervised reference model.
main_risk: Name frequency correlates with dataset curation choices and synonym structure, so establishing the causal direction requires synonym interventions rather than correlation alone.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats open-vocabulary models as compositional generalizers whose dense performance is governed mainly by visual difficulty, not by lexical statistics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive alignment quality per concept plausibly scales with the number of aligned examples seen, and dense tasks stress the weakest, least-reinforced concepts hardest.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take the per-class IoU table of any public open-vocabulary segmenter on a many-class benchmark, rank-correlate it with caption-corpus name frequency, and check the correlation against the closed-set supervised difficulty ranking.

one_line_idea: Text-to-patch similarity maps in contrastive VLMs localize by visual salience rather than by language: irrelevant text queries still highlight the same salient object.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Patch-text similarity heatmaps are widely used as evidence that contrastive VLMs ground language spatially, and qualitative figures usually show queries for objects that are also the most salient image content.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large component of these heatmaps is query-independent salience, so grounding demonstrations conflate language conditioning with generic foreground detection.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring the correlation between similarity maps for the correct query and for mismatched or nonsense queries will reveal high query-invariance on single-salient-object images, and reported grounding metrics will drop sharply on images with multiple co-salient objects.
why_important: If dense grounding is partly salience masquerading as language understanding, methods built on these maps inherit a failure mode that appears exactly when language conditioning matters most, in multi-object scenes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Salience confounds are acknowledged informally, but a quantitative decomposition of patch-text maps into query-invariant and query-dependent components may not have been carried out.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a set of images, compute similarity maps under correct, wrong-category, and pseudo-word queries; decompose map variance into query-invariant and query-dependent parts; and relate the query-dependent share to grounding accuracy.
main_risk: Softmax normalization choices across queries can artificially inflate or deflate apparent query dependence, so the decomposition must be done on raw similarities with care.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Heatmap figures are read as demonstrating that the text query causally selects the highlighted region.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive training rewards patches that align with any plausible caption content, and captions overwhelmingly describe salient foregrounds, baking a query-independent foreground prior into patch geometry.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One afternoon: fifty multi-object images, similarity maps for correct versus swapped queries from one public VLM, and a paired comparison of how often the argmax region even changes when the query changes.

one_line_idea: Class-agnostic mask generators impose a granularity prior that mismatches linguistic category boundaries, capping open-vocabulary segmentation regardless of grounding quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary pipelines rely on class-agnostic proposals whose notion of an object comes from the mask model's training distribution, while text queries can refer to merged regions, parts, or unconventional groupings.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable fraction of open-vocabulary segmentation error is granularity mismatch, cases where no available proposal aligns with the linguistically correct region, and this fraction is invariant to improvements in region classification.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Computing the best-achievable IoU over all proposals per ground-truth region will show a substantial oracle gap concentrated in part-like and merged-region categories, and this gap will persist across classifier upgrades.
why_important: It identifies where the pipeline's ceiling actually is: if granularity mismatch dominates, research should target language-conditioned proposal generation rather than better region classification.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Oracle-proposal ceilings are computed occasionally, but decomposing the ceiling by linguistic granularity type and showing its invariance to classifier quality may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a benchmark with diverse category granularities, compute per-category oracle-proposal IoU for a standard proposal set, categorize residual errors into granularity types, and verify the gap is unchanged when swapping in a stronger classifier.
main_risk: Proposal sets can be made enormous by multi-scale sampling, blurring the notion of a fixed granularity prior; the analysis needs a compute-matched proposal budget.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The pipeline view assumes proposals are sufficiently exhaustive and that scaling the VLM classifier is the binding constraint.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask models are trained on datasets with a specific object granularity convention, and nothing in their training encourages producing regions matching arbitrary linguistic construals.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, one proposal generator: report oracle-assignment mIoU next to actual mIoU, split by categories judged part-like versus canonical objects, in a single evaluation run.

one_line_idea: Dense language-grounding quality scales with caption richness (words and noun phrases per image) rather than raw pair count, making data curation for dense tasks orthogonal to curation for classification.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] VLM pretraining datasets are curated mainly for image-text semantic match, and scaling studies report image-level metrics; dense alignment is a byproduct with no dedicated curation signal.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Holding pair count fixed, pretraining on densely descriptive captions yields markedly better patch-level language alignment than sparsely captioned data, because multi-noun captions force sub-image correspondences.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Controlled pretraining runs on caption subsets matched in size but differing in noun-phrase density will produce models whose zero-shot dense segmentation differs substantially while zero-shot classification differs little.
why_important: It would give a concrete, cheap curation lever for dense-capable foundation models and explain why models with similar classification scores diverge widely on segmentation transfer.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-quality scaling work focuses on image-level filtering metrics; caption-density as the controlled variable targeting dense outcomes may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain two medium-scale contrastive models on equal-sized caption subsets stratified by noun-phrase count per caption, then evaluate both on zero-shot classification and zero-shot dense segmentation probes.
main_risk: Caption density correlates with image complexity and source domain, so subsets must be matched on image statistics to isolate the text-side variable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More pairs and better global match quality are assumed to improve all downstream granularities together.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A caption naming five objects provides implicit spatial supervision through compositional co-occurrence that a one-noun caption cannot, and dense alignment is exactly the capability starved by one-noun data.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Skip pretraining: stratify an existing model's per-image dense-probing accuracy by the caption density of its nearest pretraining neighbors as a correlational pilot before committing to controlled runs.

one_line_idea: Retrieval-based dense labeling, transferring labels from retrieved segmented neighbors in frozen VLM feature space, can rival learned open-vocabulary segmentation heads while being training-free and instantly extensible.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary segmentation methods invest in learned decoders and alignment modules, while frozen VLM features are known to support strong image-level retrieval.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Nearest-neighbor transfer of masks from a labeled support corpus via patch-level correspondence in frozen VLM space recovers most of the accuracy of trained open-vocabulary heads, indicating the heads mostly re-implement retrieval.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A pure retrieve-and-transfer pipeline with a moderately sized support set will reach within a small margin of trained open-vocabulary decoders on standard benchmarks, and its errors will overlap heavily with the trained heads' errors.
why_important: If true, the community's decoder engineering is repackaged nearest-neighbor inference, and the honest baseline for every new method should be retrieval; it also enables instant vocabulary updates without retraining.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Retrieval baselines exist for classification and few-shot segmentation, but positioning corpus-scale retrieval as a serious rival to trained open-vocabulary segmentation decoders may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a support index of segmented images embedded by a frozen VLM, label query pixels by correspondence-weighted votes from retrieved neighbors, and benchmark against published trained heads using the same backbone.
main_risk: Support-corpus coverage becomes the hidden variable; a favorable support set could overstate the claim, so coverage must be controlled and reported.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Learned alignment decoders are assumed to extract dense knowledge that simple non-parametric methods cannot reach.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frozen features already encode correspondence-quality similarity; decoders trained on limited segmentation data may mostly learn to exploit that same similarity structure with extra steps.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one benchmark, implement mask transfer from the top retrieved neighbors of each validation image using off-the-shelf features and compare mIoU to a published training-free and a published trained method.

one_line_idea: Language-grounded segmenters lean on scene-context correlations so strongly that they segment object regions correctly even when the object itself is erased, revealing context-driven rather than evidence-driven masks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contextual co-occurrence is a known shortcut for image-level recognition, but dense prediction is presumed to be anchored to local pixel evidence since output is per-pixel.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Open-vocabulary segmenters produce substantially unchanged masks for a queried object after the object's pixels are inpainted away, in proportion to the class's contextual predictability.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On images where queried objects are removed by inpainting, models will still place above-chance mask mass in the original object location, and the effect size will rank classes by contextual predictability rather than by size or frequency.
why_important: Context-driven dense predictions are a safety problem in exactly the applications that motivate open-vocabulary segmentation, such as robotics and inspection, where absence must be detectable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Object-removal probes exist for classifiers and detectors, but a class-stratified quantification for open-vocabulary dense models linking mask persistence to context statistics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct an inpainted-removal set from a segmentation benchmark, query models for the removed class, and measure residual mask mass in the original region versus a matched control region.
main_risk: Inpainting artifacts can leak object cues; artifact controls with unrelated-region inpainting of equal area are required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-pixel outputs are assumed to be grounded in per-pixel evidence, with context providing only a mild prior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The features feeding dense heads aggregate wide context by construction, and training never penalizes contextual hallucination because queried objects are almost always present in training pairs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inpaint fifty objects out of benchmark images with an off-the-shelf editor, run one open-vocabulary segmenter on the removed class, and report how often the predicted mask still lands on the vacated location.

one_line_idea: Prompt ensembling, a free win for zero-shot classification, is a mixed blessing for dense prediction: it helps region interiors but systematically blurs boundaries by averaging spatially incompatible similarity maps.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Averaging text embeddings over many prompt templates is standard practice inherited from zero-shot classification and is applied unchanged in dense pipelines.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Different templates induce systematically different spatial supports for the same class, so embedding averaging trades boundary precision for interior recall in dense tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Boundary-zone metrics will degrade or stagnate under prompt ensembling even as interior and overall IoU improve, and per-template similarity maps will show measurable spatial disagreement concentrated at boundaries.
why_important: Boundary quality drives downstream utility in editing, measurement, and medical applications; an inherited classification trick may be silently taxing exactly that property.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt ensembling effects have been studied for accuracy, but their spatial decomposition into interior versus boundary effects for dense prediction appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate single-template versus ensembled prompts for one dense zero-shot method, reporting interior IoU and boundary F-measure separately, plus inter-template spatial variance maps.
main_risk: Boundary metrics are sensitive to annotation tolerance settings, so conclusions need robustness checks across tolerance radii.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Prompt ensembling is regarded as strictly beneficial and granularity-neutral, a default hyperparameter rather than a spatial intervention.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Each template is a slightly different classifier with its own spatial response profile; averaging classifiers with misaligned decision boundaries in image space necessarily smooths the ensemble's spatial transitions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark, ten templates: compare boundary F-measure of the best single template against the ensemble in one evaluation sweep.

one_line_idea: Fine-tuning VLMs on segmentation data narrows the open vocabulary at pixel level much faster than at image level, so standard image-level forgetting checks certify models that have already lost dense open-vocabulary ability.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary segmentation systems commonly fine-tune on a closed-vocabulary segmentation dataset and verify retained generality via image-level zero-shot checks or held-out class lists.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Vocabulary forgetting is granularity-dependent: pixel-level alignment for unseen classes collapses earlier in fine-tuning than image-level alignment, because dense losses overwrite patch geometry while sparing the pooled embedding.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Tracking both image-level zero-shot accuracy and dense zero-shot IoU on unseen classes across fine-tuning checkpoints will show the dense metric collapsing substantially earlier and deeper than the image-level metric.
why_important: The community's standard evidence for retained openness would be shown to be systematically miscalibrated for dense models, affecting how every fine-tuned open-vocabulary segmenter is validated.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Catastrophic forgetting is well studied, but a granularity-resolved forgetting analysis contrasting pooled versus patch-level alignment dynamics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune a contrastive VLM with a standard segmentation head on a closed class set, checkpoint frequently, and evaluate unseen-class performance at both granularities per checkpoint.
main_risk: The dense and image-level evaluations differ in intrinsic difficulty, so collapse must be measured as relative degradation from the pretrained starting point, not absolute scores.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] If a fine-tuned model still classifies unseen categories zero-shot at image level, its open-vocabulary segmentation ability is assumed to be similarly intact.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense fine-tuning gradients act directly on the spatial feature map with many pixels per image, delivering far more parameter pressure on patch representations than the pooled path ever receives protection for.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public fine-tuned open-vocabulary segmenter and its pretrained backbone, evaluate both at both granularities on the same unseen class list, and compare the two degradation ratios.

one_line_idea: Referring expression segmentation benchmarks are largely solvable by detecting the head noun and picking the most salient instance, so reported scores overstate relational language understanding.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Referring expression datasets were collected from human games and descriptions, and human speakers systematically refer to salient objects, yet benchmark scores are interpreted as measuring compositional grounding.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A deliberately language-lobotomized baseline that extracts only the head noun and selects the largest or most salient matching instance captures a large fraction of benchmark performance, bounding how much relational understanding scores can actually reflect.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The head-noun-plus-salience baseline will achieve a substantial fraction of full-model accuracy on standard referring segmentation benchmarks, and the residual gap will concentrate in the minority of samples with multiple same-category instances.
why_important: It recalibrates the field's progress narrative: architectures credited with relational reasoning may be scoring on samples where reasoning is unnecessary, misdirecting architecture research.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Language-ablation baselines have appeared for older datasets, but a maintained, adversarially strong shortcut baseline reported alongside modern VLM-based referring models seems absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the shortcut baseline with an off-the-shelf detector and saliency ranker, evaluate on standard referring segmentation validation sets, and stratify both the baseline and a state-of-the-art model by same-category distractor count.
main_risk: Defining the head noun robustly requires parsing that itself uses language understanding; the baseline must be kept demonstrably shallow to support the conclusion.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark gains are read as improvements in grounding compositional and relational language.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dataset construction never enforced that expressions require relations to disambiguate, and human referring behavior actively minimizes required listener effort, biasing benchmarks toward shortcut-solvable samples.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run an existing open-vocabulary detector on head nouns extracted with an off-the-shelf parser, pick the highest-scoring instance, and score this pipeline on one referring benchmark validation split in a day.

one_line_idea: Referring segmentation models collapse to near-chance instance selection precisely when relational clauses are necessary, and benchmarks should be stratified by distractor count to expose this.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Aggregate referring segmentation metrics average over samples regardless of whether the image contains one or many instances of the referred category.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model accuracy conditioned on the number of same-category distractors decays steeply, with instance selection among many identical-category candidates approaching chance once appearance cues are uninformative.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-scoring public referring models stratified by same-category instance count will show a monotone, steep decline, and the decline will be steeper for relation-dependent expressions than for attribute-dependent ones.
why_important: The practical promise of referring segmentation is disambiguation among similar objects; if that regime is the failure regime, headline numbers are measuring the wrong thing.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distractor-count analyses exist in grounding literature piecemeal, but a standardized distractor-stratified reporting protocol with a relation-versus-attribute breakdown for modern models may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate validation samples of standard referring benchmarks with same-category instance counts using existing instance labels, then re-report several public models' accuracy per stratum.
main_risk: Instance-count strata correlate with scene clutter and object size, so covariate adjustment is needed before attributing decline to relational failure alone.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Steady aggregate improvements are assumed to imply improving relational disambiguation ability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggregate metrics are dominated by low-distractor samples where category detection suffices, allowing relational competence to stagnate invisibly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use existing panoptic annotations to bucket one benchmark's validation set by distractor count and re-score one public model's predictions from its released outputs without any retraining.

one_line_idea: A location-and-size prior alone, with no access to the image or the expression's content words, captures a nontrivial share of referring segmentation performance due to annotation biases toward large, central referents.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Humans photographing and describing scenes prefer centrally composed, prominent subjects, and referring datasets inherit those composition biases.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The spatial distribution of ground-truth referent masks is concentrated enough that a blind prior over location and relative size sets a surprisingly high performance floor, which published gains should be measured against but are not.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A blind baseline that outputs a dataset-fitted spatial prior mask will exceed naive chance by a wide margin on standard referring benchmarks, and the margin will vary strongly across datasets, revealing differing bias levels.
why_important: Without bias floors, cross-dataset comparisons and progress claims are uninterpretable; the floor also quantifies how much dataset construction, not modeling, contributes to scores.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Blind baselines are standard in visual question answering audits, but fitted spatial-prior floors for referring segmentation seem rarely reported for current benchmarks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit the referent mask distribution on each training split, emit the prior's maximum-a-posteriori mask for every validation sample, and tabulate overlap metrics alongside published model scores.
main_risk: A prior fitted per dataset may exploit split leakage if train and validation share source images; splits must be verified disjoint at the image level.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported referring metrics are assumed to start from a negligible chance floor, making absolute scores directly meaningful.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every stage of data collection, from photo composition to speaker choice of referent, biases referents toward the center and toward large sizes, compounding into a strong blind prior.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute the mean ground-truth mask over one training split, threshold it, apply it unchanged to every validation image, and score it in an hour.

one_line_idea: Referring segmentation models process negated expressions as if they were affirmative, segmenting exactly the object the expression excludes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contrastive text encoders are known to underrepresent negation at the sentence level, and referring pipelines inherit these encoders, yet negation handling in dense grounding is rarely evaluated.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For expressions of the form that exclude a property or location, models' predicted masks will match the affirmative reading far more often than the correct negated reading, and this failure survives across architectures including multimodal LLM-based ones.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a constructed minimal-pair suite of affirmative and negated expressions over the same images, mask agreement with the affirmative target under negated queries will be far above chance, and accuracy on negated queries will be dramatically below affirmative accuracy.
why_important: Negation is basic language; interactive segmentation interfaces will receive corrective negated instructions constantly, and silent affirmative parsing produces confidently wrong masks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Negation blindness is documented for image-text retrieval, but a controlled minimal-pair dense segmentation audit across model families may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Author minimal pairs on images with two same-category instances differing in one property, query each model with both polarity forms, and score mask assignment per polarity.
main_risk: Constructed expressions can be unnatural; a subset should be validated by human annotators to confirm the intended referent is unambiguous.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multimodal LLM-based referring models are presumed to have inherited robust negation handling from their language model component.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The grounding pathway may bypass the language model's compositional parse, matching bag-of-words content between expression and region features where negation is invisible.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifty two-instance images, one affirmative and one negated expression each, one public referring model: count how often the negated query selects the excluded object, in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Referring models fail to ground text-dependent references (objects identified by written labels in the image) even when the same system reads that text correctly in a question-answering mode, revealing an OCR-grounding integration gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Modern multimodal LLMs demonstrate strong scene-text reading, and referring interfaces are being built on them with the assumption that all their capabilities compose.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reading text and grounding masks are served by weakly integrated pathways, so expressions whose disambiguation requires reading in-image text produce near-chance instance selection despite intact reading ability verified separately.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On scenes with multiple similar objects distinguished only by visible written labels, models that answer questions about the labels correctly will nonetheless select the wrong instance when asked to segment by label, at rates far above their non-text-dependent error rate.
why_important: Text-bearing disambiguation is ubiquitous in retail, industrial, and document-adjacent scenes, and capability composition is the central promise of building dense interfaces on multimodal LLMs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scene-text understanding and referring segmentation are mature separately; a compositional audit isolating their integration for dense outputs may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate scenes with two-plus similar labeled objects, verify per-model reading via targeted questions, then evaluate label-based referring segmentation on the same scenes and compare conditional accuracies.
main_risk: Reading verification and grounding tests must use matched resolution and cropping, since text legibility is resolution-sensitive and could confound the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] If a multimodal model reads text and segments objects, the community assumes it can segment objects identified by text.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask-decoding heads typically attend to visual embeddings shaped for object semantics, while OCR ability may live in separate token pathways that the mask head never queries.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty scenes with labeled duplicate objects, one segmentation-capable multimodal model, paired reading questions and referring queries, tabulated as a two-by-two of reading success versus grounding success.

one_line_idea: No-target referring, correctly refusing to segment when the expression matches nothing, is the dominant unsolved failure mode: models confidently produce masks for absent referents.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Classic referring benchmarks guarantee the referent exists, so refusal is never trained or measured by default, while deployment queries frequently reference absent objects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Existing referring models, including those with explicit no-target training, have refusal operating points that collapse under mild domain shift, because absence detection relies on dataset-specific score calibration rather than genuine evidence assessment.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models tuned to refuse on one no-target benchmark will show large false-acceptance increases when absent-referent queries are drawn from a different distribution of plausible-but-absent expressions, revealing calibration rather than competence.
why_important: A segmentation assistant that invents referents is worse than useless in safety-relevant workflows; refusal robustness is the gating property for real interactive use.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] No-target evaluation exists, but a cross-distribution stress test distinguishing calibrated-threshold refusal from evidence-based refusal may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or take models with refusal ability, construct absent-referent queries via three generation strategies of increasing plausibility, and measure false-acceptance rates across strategies and datasets.
main_risk: Absent-referent plausibility is hard to control; generation strategies need human validation that the referent is genuinely absent yet contextually plausible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adding a no-target class or threshold during training is considered to have addressed the absent-referent problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A learned threshold on matching scores is a distribution-specific patch; nothing forces the model to represent the difference between weak evidence and absence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public no-target-capable model, swap category names in valid expressions to plausible absent categories on the same images, and measure how often a mask is still produced.

one_line_idea: Multi-target and exception referring expressions break single-instance architectural priors: models emit exactly one mask because their decoders structurally assume one referent.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Most referring architectures decode a single mask per expression, while natural instructions frequently quantify over sets, as in expressions naming all instances or excluding some.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Set-referring failure is architectural rather than linguistic: models represent the correct set internally (recoverable by probing) but the single-mask decoding interface forces an arbitrary instance choice.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Probes on intermediate representations will decode the full referent set with high accuracy on samples where the final output covers only one instance, and interface-level fixes such as iterative decoding with exclusion will recover most of the gap without retraining the backbone.
why_important: It locates the bottleneck precisely: if set information exists internally, the fix is cheap interface redesign, not new pretraining, changing the field's research agenda for instruction-driven segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-target benchmarks are emerging, but the internal-representation-versus-interface decomposition via probing may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-target expressions, train linear probes on frozen intermediate features to predict per-instance membership, compare probe recall to output recall, and test an iterative mask-then-exclude decoding wrapper.
main_risk: Probe success can overstate usable information if the probe exploits features the decoder cannot access; controls with matched-capacity probes on shuffled labels are needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Set-referring failures are attributed to insufficient multi-target training data, implying data collection as the remedy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The backbone sees rich instance evidence and the language model parses quantifiers competently; only the one-mask bottleneck discards the set structure at the very last step.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Wrap one public single-target model with iterative query rewriting that appends exclusions of already-found instances, and measure multi-target recall gain on a small annotated set.

one_line_idea: Referring accuracy is bimodal, near-ceiling when the head-noun category is unique in the image and near the distractor-chance floor otherwise, and single aggregate numbers hide this regime structure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Published referring segmentation results report single aggregate accuracies whose composition across easy and hard regimes is not visible.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Performance distributions per sample are strongly bimodal with modes governed by category uniqueness, implying aggregate improvements largely track the easy-regime share of benchmarks rather than hard-regime competence.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-sample accuracy histograms conditioned on category uniqueness will show separated modes, and progress measured across model generations will be concentrated overwhelmingly in the unique-category regime.
why_important: If hard-regime performance has been flat across generations, the field's perceived progress is a mixture artifact, and future benchmarks should report regime-conditioned metrics as primary.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Difficulty stratification exists in isolated analyses, but a longitudinal cross-generation decomposition of where referring progress actually occurred may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect released predictions or re-run several model generations on the same benchmark, split samples by category uniqueness, and chart per-regime accuracy across model release order.
main_risk: Older models may be disadvantaged by evaluation pipeline differences unrelated to competence; re-evaluation must standardize preprocessing.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Aggregate gains are interpreted as broad-based improvement including the disambiguation-hard cases.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unique-category samples reduce to open-vocabulary detection, which has improved enormously, while multi-instance disambiguation requires relational grounding that pretraining objectives never targeted.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Score two models from different generations on one benchmark stratified by category uniqueness using existing instance annotations, and compare the two per-regime deltas.

one_line_idea: Paraphrase inconsistency of referring models, where semantically equivalent expressions yield different masks, is large enough to serve as a free unsupervised error detector.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Referring models are evaluated with one expression per target, and users in deployment phrase the same request many ways; consistency under meaning-preserving rephrasing is not part of standard evaluation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Mask disagreement across paraphrases is strongly predictive of error on the original expression, so paraphrase-consistency can flag failures without any labels and can be optimized as a training signal.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sampling several paraphrases per expression and measuring inter-paraphrase mask overlap will yield a score whose correlation with ground-truth accuracy rivals or exceeds the model's own confidence outputs across multiple public models.
why_important: A label-free reliability signal enables selective prediction and self-training for referring segmentation, both currently blocked by the absence of trustworthy confidence estimates.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Self-consistency is established for language model reasoning, but its use as a dense-mask reliability estimator and training signal for referring segmentation may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate paraphrases with a language model, verify meaning preservation on a subsample by hand, run a referring model on all variants, and evaluate inter-variant IoU as a predictor of correctness against confidence baselines.
main_risk: Paraphrase generation may inject subtle meaning changes, inflating apparent inconsistency; human-validated paraphrase subsets are essential for calibration.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Model confidence scores or mask quality heads are assumed to be the natural reliability signals for referring outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confidence heads are trained on in-distribution data and miscalibrate under shift, whereas paraphrase disagreement directly measures the instability that accompanies grounding failure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark subset, five paraphrases each: correlate inter-paraphrase overlap with correctness in a day of inference.

one_line_idea: Round-trip referring, where a model generates an expression for a region and then must comprehend its own expression, exposes grounding gaps invisible to standard one-way evaluation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Referring generation and comprehension are usually evaluated as separate tasks with separate metrics, and multimodal LLMs are assumed to possess both coherently.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Round-trip failure, where a model cannot locate the region its own generated expression describes, is common and concentrates on relational and fine-grained expressions, indicating generation and comprehension use inconsistent internal groundings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Round-trip localization accuracy will be substantially below one-way comprehension accuracy on matched regions, and the discrepancy will be largest for expressions containing spatial relations.
why_important: Round-trip consistency is a prerequisite for self-supervised improvement loops and for trustworthy interactive agents; measuring it quantifies whether speaker and listener share one world model.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Speaker-listener cycle training exists in older grounding literature, but a diagnostic round-trip audit of modern segmentation-capable multimodal LLMs may not have been reported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample regions from a benchmark, have each model generate an expression per region, feed the expression back to the same model for segmentation, and compare round-trip IoU to one-way comprehension IoU on human expressions for the same regions.
main_risk: Generated expressions may be genuinely ambiguous, making round-trip failure partly a generation problem; human resolvability ratings on a subsample separate the two.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A model that both describes and segments well is assumed internally consistent between the two directions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generation is optimized for plausible text and comprehension for benchmark masks; nothing in training couples the two pathways to a shared referential semantics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one hundred regions: generate, re-comprehend, and report the round-trip IoU distribution alongside one-way IoU in a single day.

one_line_idea: Referring segmentation built on multimodal LLMs is bottlenecked by vision-encoder resolution, not language reasoning: failures concentrate on small referents regardless of expression clarity.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal LLM pipelines typically encode images at modest fixed resolutions, and referring benchmarks contain referents spanning orders of magnitude in pixel area.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Conditioning referring accuracy on referent pixel area will reveal a resolution wall below which performance collapses independently of linguistic complexity, and the wall tracks the encoder's effective patch footprint across model variants.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Accuracy-versus-referent-size curves will show a sharp knee aligned with the encoder patch size, the knee will shift with input resolution changes, and language complexity will have negligible effect below the knee.
why_important: It redirects effort: if the binding constraint is optical rather than linguistic, high-resolution token strategies matter more than better instruction tuning for dense grounding.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution sensitivity is known qualitatively, but a quantitative knee analysis tied to patch footprint and disentangled from language difficulty may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several multimodal referring models across referent-size strata with matched expression complexity, then re-evaluate at multiple input resolutions to test knee shifting.
main_risk: Small referents also correlate with clutter and occlusion; matched-complexity strata and partial-correlation analysis are needed to isolate resolution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Referring failures of multimodal LLMs are commonly attributed to grounding and reasoning limitations rather than to input resolution mechanics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A referent smaller than one vision token cannot be represented distinctly no matter how good the reasoning, making the failure mechanical and predictable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark re-binned by referent area, two input resolutions: verify the knee and its shift within a day of inference.

one_line_idea: Referring models fail on novel attribute-object combinations at segmentation time even when both the attribute and the object are individually well-grounded, exposing missing compositional binding in dense grounding.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Compositional generalization splits exist for image-level tasks, but referring segmentation benchmarks do not control whether attribute-object pairs in test expressions were seen in training.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense grounding accuracy on unseen attribute-object pairs drops sharply relative to seen pairs with matched visual difficulty, because grounding relies on memorized pair co-occurrence rather than compositional binding.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing seen-pair and unseen-pair evaluation subsets matched for object size and scene clutter will reveal a large seen-unseen gap, and the gap will persist in models whose text encoders handle the same compositions correctly in retrieval tests.
why_important: Open-world instruction following requires composing familiar words in new ways; if dense grounding is pair-memorization, the open-vocabulary promise fails exactly at its intended use.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compositional splits are standard in attribute recognition; porting them to referring segmentation with matched-difficulty controls may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine attribute-object pair statistics from training expressions, build matched seen and unseen evaluation subsets, and compare per-subset segmentation accuracy for several public models.
main_risk: Truly unseen pairs may be systematically rarer and weirder visually; matching on visual covariates is essential and imperfect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Since text encoders compose adjectives and nouns, dense grounding is assumed to inherit compositionality automatically.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The alignment between composed text embeddings and region features is only supervised where training pairs existed, so composition in text space need not transfer to composition in grounding space.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Identify twenty frequent and twenty absent attribute-object pairs from a benchmark's training expressions, collect matched test cases from validation data, and compare one model's accuracy across the two lists.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary segmentation scores are vocabulary-relative: adding plausible distractor class names to the query list collapses performance, revealing closed-set discrimination masquerading as open-set labeling.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard open-vocabulary segmentation evaluation queries exactly the benchmark's class list, so models never face the confusable near-synonyms and sibling categories an open world would present.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Measured performance is an artifact of small curated query vocabularies, and enlarging the query set with plausible distractors degrades pixel accuracy far more than it would degrade a genuinely open-set labeler.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Augmenting benchmark class lists with lexicographically plausible sibling categories will produce large, systematic mIoU drops across public models, with confusion flowing predictably to distractors that are text-embedding neighbors of true classes.
why_important: Deployment vocabularies are user-defined and large; if scores halve when the vocabulary doubles, published numbers do not predict real-world behavior at all.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Vocabulary-sensitivity analyses exist sporadically for classification; a standardized distractor-expansion stress protocol for dense benchmarks may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct distractor expansions of one benchmark's class list at several sizes using lexical resources, evaluate several models across expansion levels, and chart the degradation curves.
main_risk: Some distractors may genuinely appear in images without annotation, converting apparent errors into annotation gaps; a human audit of a confusion sample is required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported open-vocabulary results are read as evidence the model can label pixels within any reasonable vocabulary a user provides.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Softmax over the provided list makes every score relative to the list; the evaluation never tests absolute pixel-concept alignment, only discrimination within a friendly menu.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Double one benchmark's query list with sibling terms from a lexical database and re-run one public model's evaluation, comparing before and after mIoU in one pass.

one_line_idea: Per-pixel abstention, the option to label a pixel as none-of-the-provided-classes, is where all open-vocabulary segmenters fail, and it is unmeasured because benchmarks force total assignment.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary evaluation protocols assign every pixel to some queried class or a catch-all background, and real vocabularies never cover all pixels in open scenes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models given an explicit abstention option either abstain almost never or almost everywhere depending on thresholding, because contrastive similarity scores lack an absolute scale that separates covered from uncovered pixels.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On scenes where a known fraction of pixels belongs to classes deliberately withheld from the query list, the abstention precision-recall tradeoff of current models will be drastically worse than their within-vocabulary accuracy would suggest.
why_important: Total-assignment evaluation hides the failure that matters for open-world use: knowing what the vocabulary does not cover is the actual open-set competence.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Open-set recognition theory exists for classification; a rigorous pixel-level abstention benchmark with withheld-class ground truth may be missing for open-vocabulary segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create withheld-vocabulary splits of a densely annotated benchmark, query models with partial class lists plus an abstention mechanism, and score abstention quality on pixels of withheld classes.
main_risk: Abstention can be conflated with the background convention of each dataset; the protocol must distinguish semantic background from vocabulary non-coverage.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adding a threshold on maximum similarity is assumed to provide serviceable unknown-pixel rejection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Similarity scales vary per class and per image; a single threshold cannot separate coverage from non-coverage when the score distribution is not anchored to any absolute alignment meaning.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Withhold a quarter of one benchmark's classes from the query list, sweep an abstention threshold on one model, and plot abstention precision-recall on withheld-class pixels in one evaluation run.

one_line_idea: Contrastive pretraining's learned temperature makes pixel-level similarity scores relative rankings rather than probabilities, so open-set pixel calibration requires anchoring scores to an absolute alignment reference.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contrastive objectives optimize relative similarity within batches under a learned temperature, and dense pipelines consume the resulting cosine scores as if they carried absolute meaning.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pixel-label confidence derived from softmaxed cosine similarities is systematically uncalibrated in ways predictable from the contrastive objective, and calibration transfers poorly across images because the score scale is image-dependent.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Reliability analysis of pixel confidences will show large calibration error with image-dependent bias, and per-image normalization schemes anchored to reference queries will reduce calibration error substantially more than global temperature scaling.
why_important: Downstream systems consume pixel confidences for fusion and safety decisions; if the scores are only rankings, every consumer of open-vocabulary confidence is building on sand.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Calibration of zero-shot classifiers is studied at image level; the dense, per-pixel version with image-dependent scale analysis and reference-query anchoring may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute pixel-level reliability diagrams for one open-vocabulary segmenter, quantify between-image variance of the optimal temperature, and compare global versus per-image anchored calibration on held-out data.
main_risk: Pixel-level calibration ground truth inherits annotation noise at boundaries, which inflates apparent miscalibration; interior-pixel analysis should be reported separately.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A single temperature-scaling step is assumed sufficient to convert similarity maps into usable dense probabilities.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The contrastive objective never anchored similarities to any absolute event probability, and image-level normalization constants vary with scene content, making one global temperature structurally inadequate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fit a global temperature on one dataset, evaluate pixel calibration per image, and report the spread of per-image optimal temperatures in a single afternoon analysis.

one_line_idea: Vocabulary-granularity mismatch is a dominant unmeasured error source: models are marked wrong for answering at a different but correct level of the concept hierarchy, and hierarchy-aware scoring reranks methods.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark class lists mix granularities, and open-vocabulary evaluation counts a superordinate or subordinate answer as fully wrong even when it is semantically true of the pixel.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial fraction of measured open-vocabulary segmentation error consists of hierarchy-consistent answers, and correcting the metric with hierarchy-aware credit changes method rankings because methods differ in granularity bias.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-scoring confusion data against a curated class hierarchy will reveal that hierarchy-consistent confusions constitute a large error share, unevenly across methods, producing rank changes among published systems.
why_important: Metrics that punish truthful answers at the wrong granularity distort method development toward benchmark-specific naming conventions rather than genuine pixel understanding.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hierarchy-aware metrics exist for classification; systematic application to open-vocabulary segmentation with method-ranking consequences may be unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Map one benchmark's classes into an existing lexical hierarchy, re-score several public models' predictions with hierarchy-consistent credit, and compare rankings under both metrics.
main_risk: Hierarchy construction involves judgment calls that could be tuned to favor a conclusion; the hierarchy must be fixed from an independent lexical resource before scoring.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Exact-match class scoring is treated as a neutral convention with no material effect on cross-method conclusions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models trained on differing caption distributions acquire different default granularities, so exact-match scoring encodes a hidden preference for whichever granularity the benchmark happens to use.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one model's per-pixel confusions on one benchmark, mark which confusions are ancestor-descendant pairs in a lexical database, and report the hierarchy-consistent share of total error in a day.

one_line_idea: Synonym inconsistency is a cheap unforgiving audit: querying the same class by different correct names yields materially different masks, and consistency across synonyms could be enforced as a free constraint.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Users can name a concept many ways, and text encoders embed synonyms at unequal distances from visual features, yet benchmarks fix one canonical name per class.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Mask variation across synonyms of the same class is large, systematic, and predictable from caption-frequency differences between the synonyms, and enforcing synonym consistency at inference improves accuracy without any training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-class synonym sweeps will show IoU spreads that rival the gaps between competing published methods, and aggregating masks across synonyms will outperform the canonical-name query on average.
why_important: Synonym instability means reported scores depend on the benchmark's naming luck, and real users will experience unpredictable quality depending on word choice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is well known for templates; a synonym-level dense-consistency audit with an inference-time aggregation remedy may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect validated synonym sets for benchmark classes, evaluate one model per synonym, quantify per-class IoU spread, and test synonym-ensemble aggregation against canonical-name performance.
main_risk: Some synonyms carry genuine sense differences in context; synonym sets need human validation for referential equivalence in the benchmark's domain.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Class-name choice is treated as a fixed benchmark detail rather than a variable of the same magnitude as method differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Each name is a different point in text space with its own alignment history in pretraining, so nominal synonymy provides no guarantee of alignment equivalence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Five synonyms for ten classes, one model, one benchmark: report per-class IoU spread across synonyms within a single day of inference.

one_line_idea: Rare-class pixel labeling is governed by name statistics rather than visual difficulty: classes with common visual appearance but rare names underperform classes with rare appearance but common names.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Both visual rarity and lexical rarity vary across benchmark classes, and standard analyses do not separate the two when explaining per-class open-vocabulary performance.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Lexical rarity dominates visual rarity as a predictor of open-vocabulary dense accuracy, in contrast to supervised segmentation where visual factors dominate, revealing that the text tower is the binding constraint.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A two-factor analysis over classes crossed by lexical frequency and visual difficulty (estimated from a supervised model) will attribute more open-vocabulary variance to the lexical factor, and renaming rare-name classes to frequent synonyms will lift their scores.
why_important: It identifies which tower to fix: if the text side binds, dense open-vocabulary progress should come from lexical-coverage interventions, not bigger vision encoders.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frequency effects are studied broadly, but the lexical-versus-visual factorial decomposition for dense labeling with a renaming intervention may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score classes on lexical frequency and supervised-model difficulty, evaluate open-vocabulary per-class IoU, fit the two-factor model, then run the frequent-synonym renaming intervention on the rare-name cell.
main_risk: Lexical and visual rarity correlate in the world; the factorial design needs enough off-diagonal classes to have statistical power.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-class failures of open-vocabulary segmenters are usually narrated as visual difficulty, mirroring supervised intuition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The vision tower has seen every common visual pattern regardless of naming, but the alignment between a name and pixels can only form where captions used that name.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pick ten visually easy but rarely named classes, rename each to its most frequent synonym or paraphrase, and measure the IoU delta on one model in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Unseen-category generalization claims in open-vocabulary segmentation are inflated because unseen classes are visually near seen ones; stratifying by visual distance to the seen set reveals sharply weaker true generalization.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Zero-shot segmentation protocols split classes into seen and unseen sets, typically by random or legacy convention, without controlling visual similarity between the sets.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reported unseen-class performance is concentrated on unseen classes with near neighbors in the seen set, and performance decays steeply with feature-space distance from the seen classes, exposing interpolation rather than generalization.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Binning unseen classes by embedding distance to the nearest seen class will show a strong monotone performance decline, and re-splitting benchmarks to maximize seen-unseen separation will drop headline unseen mIoU substantially.
why_important: The field cites unseen-class scores as evidence of open-world readiness; if they measure interpolation distance, deployment on genuinely novel domains will disappoint predictably.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Similar critiques exist for zero-shot classification splits; a distance-stratified audit with adversarially separated re-splits for dense benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute seen-unseen class distances in a neutral feature space, stratify published unseen-class results by distance, and construct one maximum-separation re-split for re-evaluation of public models.
main_risk: Distance depends on the embedding space chosen; conclusions should be checked across at least two independent feature spaces.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Unseen-class metrics are read as measuring category-level generalization, with split composition assumed innocuous.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Random splits of correlated category inventories almost guarantee near-duplicate concepts across the seen-unseen boundary, so the protocol was never able to measure what it claims.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one benchmark and one public model, plot unseen-class IoU against nearest-seen-class embedding distance using released per-class results, requiring no new training.

one_line_idea: Anomaly segmentation via abstract text queries fails because contrastive text encoders cannot ground non-referential language: queries like unusual or out-of-place behave as near-noise directions in alignment space.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A tempting interface for open-set anomaly segmentation is to query VLMs with abstract terms describing unusualness, and contrastive training pairs captions with images where such abstract terms rarely have consistent visual referents.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Similarity maps for abstract anomaly vocabulary carry little information about actual anomalies, performing near permutation-control levels, because the text embeddings of such terms have no stable visual grounding.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On road-scene or industrial anomaly segmentation setups, abstract-query heatmaps will barely outperform maps from random control phrases of matched length, while indirect methods using per-known-class dissimilarity will clearly beat both.
why_important: Language-queried anomaly detection is an appealing product surface; establishing that the direct interface is vacuous redirects effort toward structured negative-vocabulary approaches.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anomaly segmentation and VLM grounding are separately mature; a controlled demonstration that abstract queries are unground-able with matched controls may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare abstract-query maps, random-phrase control maps, and known-class-dissimilarity maps on one anomaly segmentation benchmark under identical backbones and normalization.
main_risk: Some abstract terms may weakly correlate with anomaly context through caption usage; multiple abstract phrasings and careful controls are needed before declaring the direction vacuous.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] If a VLM understands a word in retrieval, practitioners assume querying that word densely produces a meaningful spatial map.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Grounding requires consistent visual referents during pretraining, and unusualness is context-relative with no stable appearance, so no alignment could have formed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten abstract anomaly phrases versus ten random phrases on one anomaly benchmark with one backbone: compare pixel-level detection metrics between the two groups in one run.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary segmentation degradation in specialist domains is driven more by the text tower than the vision tower: domain terms are poorly embedded, and text-side interventions recover more than image-side ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary segmenters transfer poorly to medical, aerial, and industrial imagery, and the standard explanation emphasizes visual domain gap.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For a meaningful share of specialist-domain failure, the vision features already separate the relevant structures, but domain terminology embeds far from those features, so text-side fixes (definitional paraphrases, glossary-augmented prompts) outperform image-side adaptation at equal cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Linear probes on frozen vision features will show high separability of domain structures even where language-queried labeling fails, and paraphrase-based text interventions will close more of the gap than lightweight visual adapters at matched parameter budgets.
why_important: Domain adaptation budgets are finite; knowing which tower binds determines whether teams should collect pixel labels or engineer domain-aware prompting and text adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Tower-attribution analyses exist for classification transfer; the dense specialist-domain version with matched-budget intervention comparison may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one specialist dense benchmark, measure frozen-feature probe separability, then compare glossary-paraphrase prompting against a small visual adapter trained with the same annotation budget.
main_risk: Specialist benchmarks are small, so probe and adapter comparisons need careful cross-validation to avoid noise-driven conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Specialist-domain failure is attributed to unseen visual statistics, implying image-side adaptation as the default remedy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web pretraining includes vast weakly labeled specialist imagery seen without specialist vocabulary, so visual patterns may be encoded while the domain's technical names never got aligned.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One medical or aerial benchmark: fit a linear probe on frozen patch features versus run language queries with technical names, and compare the two accuracy levels in a day.

one_line_idea: Scaling the query vocabulary to encyclopedic size produces confusion patterns predictable from text-embedding neighborhoods alone, enabling a text-only forecast of dense failure before running any image.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real deployments imply query vocabularies of thousands of names, while benchmark evaluations use dozens to a few hundred, leaving large-vocabulary dense behavior uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] As vocabulary grows, pixel-label errors become dominated by text-space neighbor confusions whose structure is computable from the text encoder alone, so a text-only audit can forecast which additions will damage which existing classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The confusion mass between class pairs under large vocabularies will correlate strongly with their text-embedding proximity, and a text-only predictor will forecast per-class degradation from vocabulary growth with useful accuracy.
why_important: A predictive text-only audit would let practitioners design safe vocabularies without expensive dense evaluation, and would formalize how open the current open-vocabulary systems really are.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Vocabulary-scaling stress tests and text-side confusion forecasting for dense prediction appear not to have been combined into a validated audit tool.
