minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one model on one benchmark under nested vocabularies from tens to thousands of names, record per-class degradation, and regress it on text-embedding neighborhood crowding computed offline.
main_risk: At large vocabularies many added names genuinely appear in images, mixing true detections with confusions; analysis must separate the two with annotation spot-checks.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Vocabulary size is assumed roughly neutral, with performance a property of the model rather than of the queried list.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Softmax competition among text neighbors grows with list size by construction, so crowding in text space must eventually govern errors regardless of visual evidence quality.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three nested vocabularies (benchmark list, five-fold expansion, twenty-five-fold expansion) on one model and benchmark, with per-class degradation regressed on text-neighbor crowding, in two days.

one_line_idea: High-norm outlier patch tokens in VLM vision towers carry global rather than local content, and filtering or reassigning them yields free dense-prediction gains across methods.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision transformers have been observed to develop high-norm tokens that serve as global computation slots, and dense pipelines consume all patch tokens as if each represented its spatial location.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In contrastively trained VLMs specifically, such outlier tokens are common, spatially unstable, and measurably harmful to language-queried dense prediction, and simple norm-based detection plus neighborhood reassignment recovers consistent accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Masking or reassigning detected outlier tokens will improve zero-shot segmentation metrics across several training-free methods and backbones, with gains concentrated in image regions where outliers cluster.
why_important: A backbone-level artifact that taxes every downstream dense method is worth one definitive characterization and a drop-in remedy usable by the whole ecosystem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The outlier-token phenomenon is documented for self-supervised models; its specific prevalence, geometry, and dense-task cost in contrastive VLMs plus a training-free fix may be uncharted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Detect high-norm tokens across VLM checkpoints, quantify their spatial information via local probing, and A-B test outlier reassignment inside two training-free segmentation methods.
main_risk: Outlier tokens may also carry information some methods exploit; removal could help some pipelines and hurt others, requiring method-stratified reporting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Patch tokens are implicitly trusted as spatially faithful local descriptors across the dense-prediction literature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in a global contrastive objective penalizes a token for abandoning its location to serve global aggregation, so spatial faithfulness is an unenforced assumption.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one training-free method, one benchmark: compare metrics with and without norm-thresholded token reassignment in a single afternoon.

one_line_idea: VLM patch features lack mid-range context integration: they are simultaneously too global for instance boundaries and too local for stuff coherence, and the missing scale is measurable and fixable at inference.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense predictions from frozen VLM features exhibit both boundary bleeding and fragmented stuff regions, two symptoms usually treated separately with ad hoc post-processing.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Both symptoms share one cause: the effective receptive field distribution of VLM patch features has a deficit at intermediate scales, and inference-time multi-scale feature mixing targeted at that deficit fixes both symptoms simultaneously.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Effective-receptive-field measurements will show a bimodal local-plus-global profile with a mid-scale gap, and injecting mid-scale aggregation will jointly improve boundary metrics and stuff-region coherence, whereas single-scale smoothing trades one for the other.
why_important: It unifies two nuisance failure modes into one measurable representational deficit with a principled remedy, replacing per-symptom heuristics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Receptive-field analyses exist for CNNs and ViTs generically; connecting a mid-scale deficit specifically to dual dense-failure symptoms in VLMs may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate effective receptive fields of patch features via gradient or perturbation methods across scales, then evaluate scale-targeted feature mixing against uniform smoothing on segmentation benchmarks.
main_risk: Effective receptive field estimation is noisy for transformers with attention sinks; multiple estimation methods should agree before the deficit is claimed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Boundary bleed and stuff fragmentation are treated as separate artifacts requiring separate post-processing tricks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Self-attention offers direct global mixing and patch embedding offers strict locality, but no architectural component enforces the intermediate neighborhood integration that segmentation needs most.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare uniform smoothing against two-scale targeted mixing on one benchmark and one backbone, checking whether only the targeted variant improves boundaries and stuff coherence together.

one_line_idea: Language-queried dense prediction inherits texture bias: pixel labels follow texture over shape in cue-conflict scenes, and the bias is stronger densely than at image level within the same model.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Texture bias is established for image-level classification in CNNs and studied in transformers, but its dense, per-pixel expression in language-grounded segmentation is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-pixel language alignment relies on local texture statistics more than image-level classification does, so cue-conflict stimuli will flip dense labels toward texture at higher rates than they flip the same model's global label.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On synthesized shape-texture conflict scenes, the fraction of pixels labeled by texture will exceed the model's image-level texture-choice rate, and the gap will widen for smaller query regions.
why_important: Dense texture bias predicts systematic failures on camouflage, material variation, and stylized imagery, and implies image-level bias audits understate dense-model risk.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cue-conflict methodology is standard at image level; its granularity-resolved comparison within one model may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate cue-conflict scenes by neural style transfer over segmentation ground truth, query models densely and globally with the same class vocabulary, and compare texture-choice rates across granularities.
main_risk: Style transfer introduces artifacts that may themselves drive labels; multiple conflict-generation methods should corroborate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Bias profiles measured at image level are assumed to characterize the model at every output granularity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pooling can average away local texture votes to recover shape at image level, but per-pixel outputs expose the raw local features where texture dominates.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifty style-transferred scenes, one model, dense versus global queries: compare texture-following rates at the two granularities in one day.

one_line_idea: Resolution-scaling tricks for dense inference silently corrupt text alignment: interpolating position embeddings improves geometry while drifting patch features away from the text tower's expected distribution.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense pipelines routinely run VLM vision towers above native pretraining resolution via position-embedding interpolation, evaluating only end-task metrics that conflate geometric and alignment effects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Position-embedding interpolation shifts the patch-feature distribution off the manifold the text alignment was calibrated to, producing class-dependent alignment drift that partially cancels the geometric gains, especially for classes whose scores were marginal.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing per-class score changes under resolution scaling will reveal classes that lose alignment even as boundary metrics improve, and matching the feature distribution back via lightweight recalibration will recover those losses.
why_important: Every high-resolution dense deployment of VLMs uses this trick; understanding its alignment tax turns an invisible tradeoff into a controllable one.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution interpolation is treated as a solved engineering detail; its text-alignment side effects for dense prediction may never have been isolated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a model across resolutions, decompose changes into localization and classification components per class, and test whether feature-distribution recalibration recovers classification-component losses.
main_risk: Localization and classification components are not perfectly separable in mask metrics; the decomposition method must be validated on synthetic cases first.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher inference resolution is assumed monotonically beneficial for dense tasks whenever compute allows.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The text tower was aligned to features from one positional geometry; interpolation changes the vision tower's internal statistics in ways the frozen text side cannot follow.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model at native and doubled resolution on one benchmark: per-class score deltas split by an oracle-mask classification test, isolating alignment drift within a day.

one_line_idea: Sliding-window dense inference produces label inconsistencies for the same object across windows, and lightweight global conditioning eliminates a class of errors that post-hoc blending merely hides.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] High-resolution open-vocabulary segmentation commonly processes overlapping windows independently and blends logits, discarding scene-level context per window.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Window-local ambiguity resolves differently across windows for the same object, creating contradictions that blending averages into low-confidence mush rather than resolving, and injecting cheap global context tokens into each window resolves them at the source.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Auditing objects spanning multiple windows will show materially different per-window label distributions, and global-token conditioning will reduce cross-window contradiction rates and improve whole-object IoU beyond what any blending schedule achieves.
why_important: Windowed inference is the default path to high resolution; quantifying and fixing its contextual blindness improves every system that scales this way.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Blending schedules are engineering folklore; a contradiction-rate metric and a global-conditioning fix for language-queried windows may be unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument windowed inference to log per-window class posteriors for objects crossing window boundaries, define a contradiction metric, and A-B test global-token injection against blending variants.
main_risk: Global conditioning increases memory and may leak large-object bias into small windows; the fix must be evaluated for regressions on window-local classes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Overlap plus smooth blending is assumed to make windowed inference equivalent to full-image inference for practical purposes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ambiguity resolution depends on context the window lacks; averaging contradictory confident answers produces neither answer, which blending cannot repair.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run windowed inference on one benchmark, measure per-object cross-window label agreement, and correlate disagreement with whole-object error in one instrumentation pass.

one_line_idea: Anisotropy of contrastive patch embeddings makes cosine similarity a low-information ranking signal densely, and simple whitening of patch features reorders and improves pixel-label decisions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contrastive representation spaces are known to be anisotropic, with embeddings concentrated in narrow cones, and dense pipelines use raw cosine similarity between patch and text embeddings as the labeling score.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Patch-embedding anisotropy is more severe than image-embedding anisotropy and injects a query-independent bias into dense scores, so post-hoc whitening or spectral normalization of patch features yields systematic dense gains without touching the text tower.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measured anisotropy will be higher for patch than pooled embeddings across VLM families, and whitening patch features will improve zero-shot segmentation while leaving image-level retrieval roughly unchanged.
why_important: A statistics-level fix that transfers across methods and backbones would raise the training-free baseline the entire subfield builds upon.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Whitening remedies are known in sentence-embedding literature; their granularity-specific analysis and application to dense VLM inference may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantify anisotropy of patch versus pooled embeddings for several VLMs, then evaluate whitened patch features inside two training-free segmentation methods on standard benchmarks.
main_risk: Whitening statistics estimated on one distribution may not transfer; per-dataset estimation could become hidden test-time tuning if not carefully protocolized.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cosine similarity in the learned space is treated as the canonical, sufficient interface between patch features and text queries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimization pressure shapes only the directions contrastive batches exercised, leaving dominant nuisance directions that cosine similarity weights equally with signal directions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Estimate a whitening transform from unlabeled images for one backbone and re-run one training-free method on one benchmark, comparing scores in a single afternoon.

one_line_idea: Multimodal LLMs contain more spatial detail than their language outputs use: pixel-probing their vision features beats their own verbalized dense answers, locating dense failure at the interface rather than in perception.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal LLMs perform poorly on fine-grained localization queries relative to specialist dense models, and this is commonly attributed to weak visual perception.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Linear or shallow probes on the frozen visual token stream inside a multimodal LLM recover substantially more dense information (boundaries, part locations, instance separation) than the model's own generated answers express, demonstrating an interface bottleneck between visual tokens and language decoding.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Probe-decoded dense predictions will exceed the same model's prompted dense outputs by a wide margin on identical images, and the gap will persist across prompting strategies and model scales.
why_important: It changes the fix: if perception is intact and expression is broken, research should target decoding interfaces and output parameterizations rather than bigger vision encoders.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Probing versus prompting comparisons exist for image-level attributes; a rigorous dense-task version quantifying the perception-expression gap in current multimodal LLMs may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Freeze one open multimodal LLM, train lightweight dense probes on its visual tokens for segmentation, and compare against the model's best prompted dense performance under matched supervision budgets for prompt engineering.
main_risk: Probes receive direct dense supervision the prompted pathway lacks, so the comparison must control supervision carefully, for example by restricting probes to few-shot budgets.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Poor dense outputs from multimodal LLMs are read as evidence that their visual representations lack spatial detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Autoregressive text decoding was never trained to serialize dense spatial structure, so rich spatial information can sit unused behind an interface optimized for global semantics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Few-shot linear probe on frozen visual tokens for coarse segmentation versus prompted segmentation from the same model on the same small benchmark, compared within two days.

one_line_idea: Segmentation-capable multimodal LLMs hallucinate masks for absent objects at rates far exceeding their question-answering hallucination rates, making dense hallucination the field's most undermeasured risk.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Object hallucination in multimodal LLMs is measured for captioning and question answering, while segmentation interfaces are newer and their hallucination behavior is largely unreported.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The mask-decoding pathway bypasses whatever calibration curbs verbal hallucination, so asking a model to segment an absent object yields a confident mask more often than asking whether the object is present yields a false yes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On matched absent-object probes, mask-production rates will substantially exceed verbal false-positive rates within the same model, and produced hallucinated masks will preferentially cover contextually plausible regions.
why_important: Dense outputs feed downstream automation directly; a mask is actionable in a way a sentence is not, so dense hallucination carries outsized deployment risk.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hallucination benchmarks target text outputs; a within-model comparison of verbal versus dense hallucination on matched probes may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched probe pairs (presence question and segmentation request for the same absent object) over images with verified absences, and compare the two false-positive rates across several segmentation-capable models.
main_risk: Presence questions and segmentation requests differ pragmatically, and models may interpret a segmentation request as presupposing existence; instruction variants must control for presupposition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Hallucination mitigation progress measured on text benchmarks is assumed to transfer to all output modalities of the same model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Refusal behavior is trained into the language head, while mask decoders are trained almost exclusively on positives with no abstention target, structurally guaranteeing the asymmetry.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifty verified-absence probes on one model, both question forms: compare verbal false-yes rate to mask-production rate in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Language-grounded segmenters are internally inconsistent about amodal versus modal extent: whether occluded object parts are included depends on the query phrasing and the occluder's category, not on any coherent convention.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Segmentation datasets follow a visible-pixels convention while natural language object reference is typically amodal, referring to whole objects irrespective of occlusion.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on visible-pixel masks but language-aligned to whole-object concepts produce inconsistent occlusion handling that varies with prompt wording, occluder type, and occlusion fraction, revealing an unresolved conflict between mask supervision and linguistic semantics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On controlled occlusion suites, the amodal-versus-modal behavior of a single model will flip across paraphrases and occluder categories at high rates, and no public model will exhibit a consistent policy across the suite.
why_important: Robotics and editing consumers need a predictable extent convention; silent inconsistency corrupts measurement, grasp planning, and edit regions in ways users cannot anticipate.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Amodal segmentation is its own literature, but auditing language-queried models for extent-convention consistency may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct scenes with parametric occlusion, query models with extent-neutral and extent-explicit phrasings, and measure policy consistency per model across occlusion levels and phrasings.
main_risk: Ground-truth amodal extents require annotation or synthesis; synthetic compositing must be checked for realism artifacts that alter model behavior.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Models are assumed to follow the visible-pixel convention of their training masks uniformly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The text tower encodes whole-object semantics from captions that never mention occlusion, injecting amodal pressure that conflicts with modal mask supervision on a per-sample basis.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Thirty composited occlusion scenes, two phrasings each, one model: tabulate how often predicted extent includes occluded regions and whether the policy is stable, in a day.

one_line_idea: Aspect-ratio deviation from pretraining crops damages dense predictions much more than global ones: padding, squeezing, and tiling choices at inference are a silent variance source dense benchmarks never control.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] VLM vision towers are pretrained predominantly on square crops, while dense benchmarks contain diverse aspect ratios handled by various padding, resizing, and cropping conventions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense metrics degrade nonlinearly with aspect-ratio distortion and the degradation exceeds the corresponding image-level effect, so unreported preprocessing choices contribute materially to cross-paper dense score differences.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping aspect-handling strategies over the same model and benchmark will produce dense-metric spreads comparable to published method gaps, while image-level metrics vary far less under the same sweep.
why_important: If preprocessing contributes method-gap-sized variance, dense leaderboards partially rank preprocessing conventions, and reproducibility requires mandatory preprocessing disclosure.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Preprocessing sensitivity is folklore, but a quantified granularity-contrasted audit attributing dense score variance to aspect handling may be unavailable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one model on one benchmark under square-pad, stretch, center-crop, and tile strategies, reporting dense and image-level metric spreads side by side.
main_risk: Optimal aspect handling may interact with model architecture, limiting generality; several backbone families should be included before drawing field-level conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Aspect handling is treated as an implementation detail beneath the reporting threshold.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Position-embedding geometry and object-shape statistics both shift with distortion, and dense outputs expose every local consequence that global pooling would have averaged away.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Four preprocessing variants, one model, one benchmark: dense metric spread versus image-level spread in one day of inference.

one_line_idea: Template context words in prompts spatially bias dense predictions: boundary pixels are more sensitive to prompt wording than interior pixels, so prompt choice partially determines boundary placement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense zero-shot pipelines embed class names inside prompt templates inherited from classification, and template effects are evaluated only through aggregate accuracy.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Template variation moves decision boundaries in image space non-uniformly, with pixel-flip probability concentrated near region boundaries, meaning boundary localization is partly a prompt artifact rather than purely a visual inference.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-pixel label-flip maps across templates will show flip probability decaying with distance from ground-truth boundaries, and boundary-metric variance across templates will exceed interior-metric variance by a large factor.
why_important: Applications that consume boundaries (measurement, editing, medical delineation) are unknowingly consuming prompt-dependent boundaries, which undermines their reproducibility.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is quantified for accuracy; its spatial anatomy within images may be uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one model with many templates on one benchmark, compute per-pixel flip statistics as a function of boundary distance, and decompose metric variance into boundary and interior contributions.
main_risk: Boundary pixels are intrinsically ambiguous, so flip concentration there may partly reflect genuine ambiguity; comparison against a supervised model's flip profile under input noise provides a baseline.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Prompt effects are assumed spatially uniform, shifting scores globally without changing where boundaries fall.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Templates shift class prototypes in text space, and pixels nearest the decision surface, which are boundary pixels, flip first under any prototype shift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten templates, one model, one benchmark subset: plot flip probability against distance-to-boundary in a single analysis pass.

one_line_idea: The best-aligned layer for dense prediction differs systematically by query type (things versus stuff, objects versus parts), so any single-layer feature choice is guaranteed suboptimal and query-adaptive layer selection is free accuracy.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training-free dense methods extract features from one fixed layer chosen by validation, applying that choice uniformly across all queries and categories.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Optimal extraction depth is a stable function of query semantics, with stuff and material queries peaking earlier and object and part queries peaking later, enabling a lightweight query-conditioned layer router that beats every fixed layer.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-category layer sweeps will reveal systematically different optima clustered by semantic type across backbones, and a router selecting depth from the text query alone will outperform the best single layer on full benchmarks.
why_important: It converts a hidden hyperparameter into a principled, query-dependent choice and adds accuracy to every training-free dense method at negligible cost.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Layer sweeps appear in ablations, but the semantic structure of per-query optimal depth and a text-conditioned router may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep layers per category on two benchmarks and two backbones, test whether optima cluster by semantic type, then train a tiny text-embedding-to-layer router on one benchmark and evaluate transfer to the other.
main_risk: Per-category optima estimated on small benchmarks are noisy; clustering claims need confidence intervals from bootstrap resampling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A single well-chosen layer is assumed adequate for all queries, with layer choice treated as a global hyperparameter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Different semantic types are computed at different depths in hierarchical networks, so the alignment between patch semantics and query semantics must peak at type-dependent depths.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Layer sweep on one backbone for ten thing classes and ten stuff classes on one benchmark: check whether the two optima distributions separate, in one day.

one_line_idea: The confusion matrix of an open-vocabulary segmenter is largely predictable from text-encoder geometry alone, before any image is processed, making text-side audits a cheap proxy for dense error analysis.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense error analysis requires expensive per-pixel evaluation, while the text embeddings of all query classes are available for free before inference.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pairwise class confusion mass in dense predictions is strongly predicted by text-embedding similarity between class names, with visual similarity adding surprisingly little once text geometry is accounted for.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Regressing empirical dense confusion rates on text-pair similarity will yield strong predictive power across benchmarks and models, and the text-only predictor will approach the accuracy of a predictor using visual class prototypes.
why_important: A validated text-only error forecast lets practitioners debug vocabularies and predict deployment confusions without dense ground truth, which most real domains lack.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Text-geometry analyses exist for retrieval; their validated use as a quantitative forecaster of dense confusion structure may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect confusion matrices from several public models on several benchmarks, regress confusion mass on text-pair similarity and on visual-prototype similarity, and compare explanatory power.
main_risk: Text and visual similarity are correlated through the alignment training itself, complicating causal attribution; the claim should stay predictive rather than causal.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense confusions are assumed to reflect visual similarity between categories, requiring image-side analysis to understand.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pixel labeling is a nearest-text-neighbor decision at its core, so crowding in text space mechanically translates into confusion regardless of visual distinctness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark: rank class pairs by text similarity, check what fraction of total confusion mass falls in the top-ranked pairs, in a few hours.

one_line_idea: Hub class names, text embeddings abnormally close to many patch features, absorb pixels from many true classes, and hubness-correction techniques from retrieval transfer directly to dense labeling as training-free gains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Hubness, where certain points become nearest neighbors to disproportionately many queries, is a known pathology of high-dimensional similarity search, and dense labeling is a nearest-text-neighbor decision per pixel.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A small set of class names act as hubs in each vocabulary, capturing pixel mass far beyond their true prevalence, and applying retrieval-style hubness corrections to the pixel-to-text assignment reduces this systematic error across models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-class predicted-versus-true pixel mass will reveal consistent absorber classes stable across images, hubness scores computed from text-patch similarity statistics will identify them a priori, and corrected assignment will improve mIoU with the largest gains on classes adjacent to hubs.
why_important: It imports a mature body of nearest-neighbor pathology theory into dense open-vocabulary prediction, explaining a recurring error pattern and providing an immediate remedy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hubness corrections are standard in cross-modal retrieval; their formulation and validation for per-pixel labeling may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute hubness statistics of class embeddings against patch-feature samples, identify absorber classes, apply inverted-softmax-style correction to dense assignment, and evaluate across two benchmarks and two models.
main_risk: Corrections calibrated on one image distribution may misfire on another; the protocol must separate correction-fitting data from evaluation data.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Over-predicted classes are explained by visual ambiguity or dataset bias rather than by a geometric pathology of nearest-neighbor assignment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-dimensional concentration effects guarantee some queries become hubs irrespective of semantics, and per-pixel assignment multiplies the pathology across millions of decisions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark: rank classes by predicted-to-true pixel mass ratio, test whether a text-side hubness score computed without labels predicts that ranking, in one afternoon.

one_line_idea: Class-name token length biases dense similarity magnitudes, so multi-word categories are systematically under- or over-predicted, and length normalization is a missing preprocessing step in every open-vocabulary pipeline.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark vocabularies mix single-word and multi-word class names, and text encoders produce embeddings whose statistics vary with token count, while dense pipelines compare all classes on one similarity scale.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Embedding norm and effective similarity scale correlate with name token length, injecting a length-dependent prior into pixel assignment that is unrelated to visual evidence and correctable by per-class score standardization.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Prediction bias per class (predicted minus true pixel share) will correlate with name token length across benchmarks and models, and per-class standardization estimated from unlabeled images will reduce both the correlation and overall error.
why_important: A mundane lexical property silently tilting dense predictions across every benchmark is exactly the kind of confound that corrupts cross-method comparisons and real deployments alike.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Length effects on sentence embeddings are documented; their downstream effect on dense pixel assignment and a standardization remedy may be unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-class prediction bias against token length for several models and benchmarks, then evaluate per-class score standardization fitted on unlabeled data.
main_risk: Token length correlates with concept specificity, which has its own frequency effects; partial correlations controlling for name frequency are required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Class-name embeddings are assumed comparable on a common similarity scale regardless of surface form.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pooling over different token counts changes embedding statistics mechanically, and nothing in contrastive training equalizes similarity scales across name lengths.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one benchmark: scatter per-class prediction bias against name token count and fit the trend, in a few hours from existing prediction dumps.

one_line_idea: Polysemous class names produce sense-blended text embeddings that corrupt dense predictions, and sense-disambiguating prompt contexts recover accuracy on quietly polysemous benchmark classes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Common benchmark class names carry multiple senses in web text, and contrastive text encoders produce a single embedding per surface form, blending senses in proportion to caption usage.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For polysemous class names, the blended embedding sits between visual senses, depressing dense accuracy relative to a sense-pinned prompt, and the accuracy loss is predictable from sense-distribution statistics in web text.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Adding brief disambiguating context to polysemous class names will improve their dense IoU markedly while leaving monosemous classes unchanged, and the per-class gain will correlate with corpus-estimated sense entropy.
why_important: It identifies a hidden per-class handicap in every benchmark and provides a zero-cost prompt-side remedy with predictable applicability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Polysemy is a classic NLP topic; its quantified dense-prediction cost and a sense-entropy-based predictor of prompt-fix gains may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify polysemous benchmark classes via a sense inventory, construct disambiguated prompts, evaluate paired vanilla-versus-disambiguated dense accuracy, and correlate gains with sense entropy estimates.
main_risk: Added context words change embeddings beyond disambiguation; monosemous control classes with equivalent added context isolate the disambiguation effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Class names are treated as unambiguous pointers to visual concepts, with polysemy considered an edge case not worth protocol changes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The encoder had no mechanism to separate senses of one surface form, so every polysemous name necessarily drags irrelevant visual sense components into pixel scoring.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten polysemous and ten monosemous classes, vanilla versus contextualized prompts, one model and benchmark: paired accuracy comparison in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Contrastive text encoders barely encode spatial-relational words: removing them from referring expressions leaves the text embedding nearly unchanged, mechanistically explaining relation-blind dense grounding.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Referring pipelines that use contrastive text towers must represent relational words to ground relational expressions, yet contrastive training rewards mostly object-noun alignment because captions and images match through content words.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The embedding displacement caused by deleting or swapping spatial-relational words is small relative to displacement from content-word changes, and this text-side insensitivity quantitatively predicts each model's relational grounding failure rate.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across encoders, relational-word edits will move embeddings far less than content-word edits of matched frequency, and models ranked by this text-side sensitivity will rank identically on relation-dependent grounding accuracy.
why_important: It provides a mechanistic, text-measurable root cause for a prominent dense failure, enabling encoder selection and targeted text-tower fixes without expensive dense evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Word-level sensitivity analyses exist for language models; connecting relational-word insensitivity in contrastive towers to dense grounding outcomes may be unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct minimal-edit expression sets varying relational versus content words, measure embedding displacement per edit type across encoders, and correlate with relation-stratified grounding accuracy of systems using those encoders.
main_risk: Grounding systems add fusion modules that could compensate for text-tower insensitivity, weakening the correlation; system-level confounds need documenting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Relational grounding failure is attributed to the vision side or the fusion module, with the text embedding assumed to faithfully carry the expression's relational content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contrastive objectives optimize what distinguishes captions across images, and spatial relations rarely do, so the encoder had no pressure to preserve them.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifty expressions, three edit types, two encoders: compare displacement distributions in hours, then spot-check against published relation-stratified results.

one_line_idea: Negation invariance of contrastive text embeddings transfers directly into dense prediction: negated queries produce near-identical similarity maps to affirmative ones, and the embedding distance between a phrase and its negation predicts which models can be fixed by prompting alone.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contrastive text encoders are reported to underrepresent negation in retrieval settings, and dense pipelines inherit these encoders without negation-specific evaluation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The cosine distance between affirmative and negated forms of the same query is a strong predictor of a system's dense negation accuracy, separating systems fixable by prompt rewording from systems requiring text-tower surgery.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Similarity-map correlation between negated and affirmative queries will be near unity for encoders with small negation displacement, and dense negation accuracy across systems will track the text-side displacement metric closely.
why_important: A text-only diagnostic that predicts dense negation capability lets practitioners audit systems cheaply and choose remediation strategies rationally.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Negation studies focus on retrieval accuracy; a displacement-based diagnostic validated against dense outcomes may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute negation displacement for several text towers, measure dense negation accuracy of matching systems on a minimal-pair suite, and evaluate the diagnostic's predictive power.
main_risk: Some systems process queries through language models before the grounding step, decoupling the contrastive tower's geometry from system behavior; system architecture must be catalogued.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Negation failures are treated as a monolithic model capability gap rather than a measurable, localizable text-geometry property.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If negation never changes the text embedding, no downstream component can recover the lost polarity, making the text-side measurement a hard ceiling on dense behavior.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty query pairs, three encoders, dense maps from one pipeline per encoder: correlate map similarity with embedding displacement in a day.

one_line_idea: Attribute-binding failure is text-side measurable: swapped-attribute expressions embed nearly identically in contrastive towers, and this bag-of-words geometry upper-bounds dense binding accuracy no matter how good the vision tower is.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Compositional binding failures, where models confuse which attribute belongs to which object, are documented for image-text retrieval, and dense grounding pipelines reuse the same text towers.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The embedding distance between attribute-swapped expression pairs upper-bounds dense binding performance: systems whose text towers collapse swapped pairs cannot exceed chance on binding-critical dense queries, and the bound is tight empirically.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Plotting dense binding accuracy against text-side swap displacement across systems will show a tight envelope with no system materially above the bound line, and interventions that increase swap displacement will raise the dense ceiling correspondingly.
why_important: Establishing a text-geometry ceiling redirects binding research from vision-side architecture tweaks to text-tower compositionality, where the binding information is being destroyed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Binding critiques exist at retrieval level; the formulation as a quantitative ceiling on dense grounding with envelope analysis may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble binding-critical dense test cases with two-object attribute swaps, measure system accuracy and text-tower swap displacement, and test the envelope hypothesis across diverse systems.
main_risk: Systems with generative language components may re-parse expressions and escape the contrastive ceiling; such systems test the hypothesis's scope conditions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Binding failures in dense grounding are blamed on vision-language fusion, with the text representation presumed adequate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Information deleted at the text encoding stage is unrecoverable downstream, so a collapsed text geometry mathematically caps every subsequent computation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty swapped-pair scenes, three systems with different text towers: check whether any system beats chance while its tower collapses the pairs, in a day or two.

one_line_idea: Cross-lingual dense inconsistency, where translated class names yield different masks on the same image, is large, systematic, and a free multilingual audit for text-tower quality in dense pipelines.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multilingual users query dense systems in many languages, and multilingual text towers embed translation-equivalent names at unequal alignment quality, yet dense evaluation is monolingual by default.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Mask agreement across translated queries varies widely by language and class, tracks language share in pretraining text, and cross-lingual disagreement on unlabeled images predicts per-language dense accuracy without any labels.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-language dense accuracy will correlate strongly with label-free cross-lingual mask agreement measured on unlabeled data, validating disagreement as an unsupervised audit, and low-resource languages will show both lower accuracy and lower agreement.
why_important: A label-free per-language quality estimate enables responsible multilingual deployment of dense systems in domains where no labeled data exists in the target language.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multilingual gaps are documented for retrieval; using cross-lingual dense disagreement as a validated unsupervised accuracy predictor may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Translate benchmark class lists into several languages with human verification, evaluate dense accuracy per language, measure cross-lingual agreement on a disjoint unlabeled set, and test the prediction relationship.
main_risk: Translation introduces sense shifts for some classes; human verification and back-translation checks are essential to keep name equivalence.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multilingual encoders are assumed to deliver roughly language-neutral dense behavior for common concrete nouns.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Alignment quality per name depends on per-language caption exposure, which varies by orders of magnitude, and dense prediction amplifies small alignment differences into visible mask changes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Five languages, twenty classes, one model: mask agreement matrix on fifty unlabeled images versus per-language accuracy on a small labeled set, within two days.

one_line_idea: Dense grounding models resolve frame-of-reference ambiguity by always choosing the viewer-centric reading, and benchmarks silently reward this because annotators did too, hiding a genuine ambiguity the field has never measured.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Spatial expressions like left-of are ambiguous between viewer-centric and object-centric frames, and grounding datasets do not annotate which frame the speaker intended.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models exhibit a rigid viewer-centric policy regardless of contextual cues that humans use to switch frames, and measured spatial-grounding accuracy overstates competence because benchmark annotations share the same default.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On stimuli where object-centric and viewer-centric readings pick different referents, models will choose viewer-centric at near-ceiling rates even when the expression strongly cues the object-centric frame, and human annotators will show substantially more context-driven switching.
why_important: Robotics instructions routinely use object-centric frames; a rigid viewer-centric policy produces confidently wrong groundings in embodied settings while benchmark scores stay high.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frame of reference is studied in psycholinguistics; a controlled audit of dense grounding models' frame policies with human comparison may be absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct frame-disambiguating scenes with objects that have intrinsic orientations, collect human frame choices as reference, and measure model frame choices across cue conditions.
main_risk: Constructing scenes where frames genuinely diverge requires oriented objects and careful geometry; poor stimulus design would blur the frames rather than oppose them.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Spatial-relation accuracy numbers are read as understanding of spatial language, without frame ambiguity entering the discussion.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web training data overwhelmingly reflects viewer-centric photo descriptions, giving models no signal that other frames exist, while benchmarks inherited the same bias so the gap never surfaced.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Thirty oriented-object scenes with divergent frame readings, one grounding model: tabulate frame choices against the cued frame in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Dense grounding handles canonical categorical relations but fails graded and metric spatial language: nearest, halfway, and almost-touching ground at near-chance despite high scores on left-right-above benchmarks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Spatial grounding evaluation is dominated by a small closed set of categorical prepositions, while natural instructions frequently use graded, comparative, and metric spatial descriptions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models implement categorical relations as learned 2D templates and possess no graded spatial computation, so performance collapses precisely when the relation requires comparing continuous distances rather than matching a template.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A stratified suite from categorical to graded to metric relations will show a steep performance cliff at the categorical-to-graded transition across model families, with metric relations near chance even for models saturating categorical subsets.
why_important: Instruction-following robots and editors need graded spatial language constantly; the field's chosen evaluation set has hidden a capability cliff exactly where deployment needs begin.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual graded-relation failures are anecdotal; a systematic difficulty-ordered spatial-language taxonomy with cliff localization may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a relation taxonomy with matched scenes across strata, evaluate several grounding models per stratum, and locate each model's performance cliff.
main_risk: Graded relations have softer ground truth requiring tolerance bands or human agreement distributions rather than binary correctness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Rising scores on standard spatial benchmarks are taken to indicate broadly improving spatial-language understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Categorical templates are learnable from co-occurrence statistics without any distance computation, so benchmark success never required the capability that graded language demands.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty scenes each for one categorical and one metric relation with unambiguous ground truth, one model: compare the two accuracies in a day.

one_line_idea: Relational grounding accuracy decays superlinearly with scene clutter because models approximate relations with global position priors that collapse when many candidates occupy every image region.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Spatial grounding is evaluated on datasets whose scenes are moderately cluttered, and per-sample clutter is not a standard reporting dimension.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models ground relations via absolute image-position priors (left-of resolving to left-half-of-image) rather than relative geometry between the mentioned objects, a strategy whose accuracy collapses combinatorially as clutter grows.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Accuracy versus distractor count will decay faster than an ideal relative-geometry observer's decay, and error analysis will show predicted referents clustering in the image region named by the preposition regardless of the anchor object's actual position.
why_important: It exposes that measured relational competence is an absolute-position heuristic, predicting sharp failure in dense real scenes such as shelves, crowds, and desks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Position-bias analyses exist for question answering; a mechanistic absolute-versus-relative diagnosis for dense relational grounding may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct scenes varying distractor count with anchor objects placed against the prior (anchor on the right for left-of queries), and test whether predictions follow the anchor or the absolute region.
main_risk: Synthetic scene construction may itself introduce placement regularities; randomized placement protocols and naturalistic scene subsets should agree.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Relational benchmark accuracy is interpreted as computing geometry between the referenced objects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Absolute-position shortcuts explain most training data correctly because photographers compose scenes conventionally, so models never needed relative geometry to fit the data.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Thirty anti-prior scenes where the correct referent lies opposite the preposition's absolute region, one model: measure how often predictions follow the absolute region, in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Depth-dependent relations fail because VLM features encode little metric depth, and supplying monocular depth as an auxiliary input disproportionately repairs behind and in-front-of while leaving 2D relations unchanged, cleanly attributing the failure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Grounding expressions with depth-order relations requires 3D information that 2D-trained contrastive features are not obviously forced to represent, and dense grounding evaluations do not stratify relations by dimensionality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The error profile of dense grounding is dimensionally structured: 2D relations succeed and depth relations fail in proportion to the features' measurable depth content, and depth-input injection acts as a targeted intervention validating the causal account.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Relation-stratified evaluation will show depth relations far below 2D relations, probes will find weak metric depth in the relevant features, and adding estimated depth will lift depth relations substantially while 2D relations move negligibly.
why_important: A clean causal decomposition of spatial grounding failure by dimensionality tells system builders exactly which sensor or auxiliary model closes which capability gap.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Depth probing of vision features and grounding evaluation exist separately; the targeted-intervention causal linkage for dense relational grounding may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify a grounding benchmark by relation dimensionality, probe backbone features for depth content, and A-B test depth-channel injection in one grounding architecture.
main_risk: Depth injection changes model capacity and training, so matched-parameter control variants with shuffled depth are needed to isolate the informational contribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Spatial grounding failures are treated as one undifferentiated weakness rather than as dimensionally structured with distinct causes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in image-text contrastive training rewards metric depth encoding beyond what silhouette and occlusion cues incidentally provide, so depth relations rest on missing information.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score one public model's grounding predictions stratified into 2D versus depth-order relations using existing annotations, confirming the asymmetry before any intervention work.

one_line_idea: Relative-size references ground by image-plane area rather than real-world size: models pick the object with more pixels, failing whenever perspective makes the physically larger object smaller in the frame.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Expressions like the bigger one are common in referring data, and image-plane size diverges from physical size under perspective, but evaluations never separate the two.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense grounding models implement size comparatives as pixel-area comparisons with no depth correction, so their accuracy on size expressions inverts on perspective-conflict cases where the physically larger object is farther away.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On conflict cases, models will select the pixel-larger object at rates far above chance even when scene cues make physical size obvious to humans, and on congruent cases the same models will look spuriously competent.
why_important: Size language in embodied instruction refers to physical objects, not projections; a pixel-area heuristic produces systematic real-world errors invisible to current benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Perspective-conflict methodology is used in cognitive science; its application to auditing size-comparative grounding in dense models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or synthesize congruent and conflict scenes with verified physical-size ground truth, evaluate size-comparative expressions on both subsets, and compare accuracy inversion across models.
main_risk: Humans also partially rely on image size under impoverished cues, so human baselines on the same stimuli are needed to define the achievable ceiling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Success on size expressions in standard benchmarks is taken as understanding of object size.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pixel area is directly available in the representation while physical size requires depth inference the features likely lack, making the shortcut both easy and usually correct in benchmark data.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty perspective-conflict images, one model, size-comparative queries: count pixel-area-following choices in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Dense grounding models trained on web photos fail systematically on egocentric viewpoints, and the failure is viewpoint-distributional rather than object-level: the same objects ground fine in third-person views.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web-scraped training imagery is overwhelmingly third-person composed photography, while embodied applications supply egocentric video with hands, motion blur, and extreme viewpoints.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Grounding degradation on egocentric imagery persists after controlling for object category and image quality, indicating a viewpoint-distribution gap in dense alignment rather than a recognition gap, and small amounts of egocentric-aligned data close it disproportionately fast.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matched-object comparisons across viewpoint conditions will show large dense-grounding gaps that image-level recognition does not show, and viewpoint-targeted adaptation with modest data will recover most of the gap while general-domain data of equal size will not.
why_important: Egocentric grounding is the entry ticket for assistive and robotic applications; knowing the gap is distributional and cheaply fixable changes deployment strategy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Egocentric-versus-web domain gaps are studied for recognition; the granularity-contrast showing dense alignment suffers more, plus the targeted-data efficiency claim, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble matched-object egocentric and third-person test pairs, evaluate dense grounding and image-level recognition on both, then run matched-budget adaptation with egocentric versus generic data.
main_risk: Perfectly matching objects and contexts across viewpoints is hard; paired capture or careful covariate matching is required to avoid confounds.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Foundation-model generality is assumed to cover viewpoint variation, with egocentric treated as just another domain the scale already handles.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense alignment depends on spatial feature statistics that egocentric geometry shifts drastically, while pooled recognition features are more viewpoint-tolerant, hiding the gap from standard checks.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifty matched object instances in egocentric and third-person views, one model: compare dense grounding accuracy across conditions in two days including curation.

one_line_idea: Grounding accuracy decays multiplicatively per relational hop in nested expressions, and measuring the per-hop decay factor gives a single scalar that predicts model behavior on arbitrarily complex referring chains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Natural referring expressions nest relations (the book on the table near the window), yet benchmarks report flat accuracy without characterizing how performance scales with relational depth.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Each additional relational hop multiplies success probability by a roughly constant model-specific factor, so complex-expression performance is predictable from single-hop measurements, and apparent architecture differences on hard benchmarks reduce to differences in this one factor.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Accuracy versus hop count on controlled nested expressions will fit a geometric decay closely, the fitted factor will vary across architectures, and the factor measured on synthetic scenes will predict accuracy on naturally complex benchmark subsets.
why_important: A validated decay law converts benchmark design and model comparison for complex language into a principled measurement problem, and reveals whether any architecture achieves genuinely compositional (non-multiplicative) grounding.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compositional decay is measured in other domains; a per-hop decay-law analysis for dense referential grounding with cross-dataset prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate scenes supporting one-to-four-hop expressions with unique referents, evaluate several models per depth, fit decay curves, and validate predictions on hop-annotated natural expressions.
main_risk: Hop count correlates with expression length and scene complexity; stimulus design must vary hops while holding lexical and scene statistics constant.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Complex-expression failure is described qualitatively as models struggling with composition, without a quantitative scaling law.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If each hop is resolved by an imperfect, roughly independent matching step, the multiplicative structure follows automatically, and nothing in current architectures shares evidence across hops to beat it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Synthetic scenes at three hop depths, one model: fit the geometric decay on a few hundred samples in a day.

one_line_idea: Spatial terms function as tie-breakers, not constraints: models first shortlist referents by appearance and only consult spatial language when appearance ties, an order of operations exposable by appearance-spatial conflict stimuli.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Referring expressions combine appearance and spatial cues, and standard datasets rarely put the two in conflict, leaving the models' cue-priority structure unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense grounding operates lexicographically, appearance first and space second, so when spatial language contradicts the best appearance match, models follow appearance at high rates rather than integrating both cues probabilistically as listeners do.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On conflict stimuli where the spatially correct referent is a slightly worse appearance match, models will choose the appearance match far more often than humans, and cue-weight estimates fitted from choices will show near-zero spatial weight until appearance similarity is nearly tied.
why_important: Understanding cue integration order predicts exactly which instructions will fail and motivates architectures with calibrated cue fusion instead of implicit lexicographic shortcuts.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cue-conflict psychophysics is standard for perception; applying cue-weight estimation to dense referential grounding may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build conflict stimuli parametrically varying appearance-match strength against spatial correctness, fit cue-integration models to machine and human choices, and compare integration structure.
main_risk: Appearance-match strength must be quantified independently, for example by embedding similarity, and validated against human similarity judgments.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Models are assumed to weigh all expression cues jointly, with failures attributed to capacity rather than to a fixed cue hierarchy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Appearance matching is directly supported by contrastive pretraining while spatial matching is not, so a lexicographic policy emerges naturally from the asymmetric strength of the two pathways.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Thirty conflict scenes with two candidate referents each, one model: measure appearance-following rate against the spatial instruction in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Cross-dataset open-vocabulary evaluation partially measures label-name compatibility: renaming target-dataset classes to equally correct synonyms reranks methods, revealing name-matching as a hidden score component.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary segmentation is evaluated by transferring to datasets whose class names were chosen by annotators, and methods differ in how their training vocabulary relates to those specific names.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A meaningful share of cross-dataset score differences between methods comes from differential affinity to the target's naming conventions rather than from dense capability, and synonym-renamed re-evaluation reorders published rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-evaluating several methods under multiple equally valid renamings of target class lists will produce rank instability well beyond evaluation noise, and each method will show idiosyncratic name affinities traceable to its training vocabulary.
why_important: If rankings flip under legitimate renamings, cross-dataset leaderboards are partly lexical lotteries and their method-selection guidance is unreliable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt-template sensitivity is known; systematic synonym-renaming as a leaderboard-stability audit for dense transfer may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Produce three human-validated synonym renamings per target benchmark, re-evaluate public methods under each, and quantify rank stability with bootstrap confidence intervals.
main_risk: Some synonyms subtly change class extension; renaming sets need validation that annotation semantics are preserved.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cross-dataset mIoU differences are read as differences in generalization capability, with class naming assumed neutral.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every method's score is mediated by similarity between its learned text manifold and the specific benchmark names, an alignment of vocabularies rather than of pixels.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, two renamings, three methods: check for rank changes in a single re-evaluation sweep.

one_line_idea: Decomposing open-vocabulary segmentation error into recognition and localization components reranks methods: some celebrated systems win on localization while losing on recognition, and mIoU hides which skill improved.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] mIoU aggregates errors of fundamentally different kinds, misclassified regions and misplaced boundaries, into one number, and open-vocabulary papers rarely report the decomposition.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method rankings under recognition-only and localization-only metrics diverge substantially, and recent progress claimed as grounding improvement is disproportionately localization improvement inherited from better mask backbones.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Scoring public methods with oracle-classification (true labels, predicted masks) and oracle-localization (predicted labels, true masks) protocols will produce visibly different rankings, with temporal analysis showing recognition progress lagging localization progress.
why_important: The field allocates research effort based on what appears to be improving; a decomposed scoreboard redirects effort to the actually lagging skill.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Error decompositions exist for detection; a systematic recognition-localization decomposition with temporal trend analysis for open-vocabulary segmentation may be unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement both oracle protocols on one benchmark, score methods spanning several release years, and chart the two skill trajectories separately.
main_risk: Oracle protocols interact with method internals differently (some methods have no separable mask stage), requiring protocol adaptations documented per method.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Rising mIoU is read as improving vision-language grounding, the named contribution of most papers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: mIoU rewards both skills interchangeably, and the ecosystem's mask backbones improved rapidly, letting grounding stagnate while headline numbers climbed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two methods from different eras, both oracle protocols, one benchmark: compare skill-specific deltas in a day.

one_line_idea: Referring benchmarks contain enough annotation ambiguity that top models may already be at the inter-annotator ceiling, making current leaderboard differences unmeasurable noise.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Referring expressions collected from humans admit multiple defensible referents in cluttered scenes, and benchmark ground truth records exactly one mask per expression without agreement statistics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-annotating benchmark samples with multiple independent annotators will reveal disagreement rates comparable to the error rates of leading models, implying the effective ceiling has been reached and residual leaderboard gaps reflect fit to annotator idiosyncrasies.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Human-human agreement measured on standard validation splits will bound achievable accuracy at a level current best models approach, and model errors will concentrate on exactly the samples where humans disagree.
why_important: Chasing gains beyond the annotation ceiling wastes effort and rewards overfitting to noise; establishing the ceiling would force benchmark renewal with agreement-aware ground truth.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotation-noise ceilings are established for classification benchmarks; a rigorous agreement study for referring segmentation ground truth may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample validation subsets from standard referring benchmarks, collect several independent re-annotations per expression, compute agreement bounds, and locate current model scores relative to them.
main_risk: Annotator recruitment and instruction differences could produce artificially low agreement; the protocol must mirror original collection instructions faithfully.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Remaining headroom on referring benchmarks is assumed to represent capability gaps worth pursuing with better models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Single-annotator ground truth on ambiguous stimuli guarantees a noise floor, and model error rates near that floor are statistically indistinguishable from ceiling performance.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One hundred expressions re-annotated by three annotators each: compare disagreement rate with the current best model's error rate on the same samples.

one_line_idea: Zero-shot dense evaluation quietly permits test-distribution prompt tuning: template and vocabulary choices are optimized against the very benchmarks reported, and a strict no-peek protocol measurably deflates published-style numbers.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Papers report zero-shot dense results using templates, vocabularies, and inference tricks selected during development on the same benchmarks, a workflow that constitutes indirect test-set tuning.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The gap between development-tuned and strictly held-out prompt configurations is large enough to account for a meaningful fraction of claimed method differences in open-vocabulary segmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating public methods under prompts frozen before seeing the target benchmark (chosen on disjoint development data) will lower scores non-uniformly across methods and compress or reorder published gaps.
why_important: Zero-shot claims are the field's headline product; if they embed hidden test tuning, both absolute numbers and relative rankings mislead adopters.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Test-set reuse critiques are established for classification; a quantified prompt-tuning-leakage audit for dense zero-shot evaluation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a pre-registered prompt-selection protocol on development benchmarks, re-evaluate several methods on held-out benchmarks under frozen prompts, and compare against paper-reported configurations.
main_risk: Reconstructing each paper's exact tuned configuration is imperfect; collaboration with method authors or released configs mitigates misrepresentation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Zero-shot numbers are read as unbiased estimates of transfer performance to unseen data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every development iteration that consulted target-benchmark scores injected selection bias, and prompt spaces are large enough for that bias to be substantial.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one method, compare its paper configuration against a configuration chosen on a disjoint dataset, evaluated on the same target benchmark, in one day.

one_line_idea: Boundary-weighted evaluation reranks open-vocabulary segmenters because interior-pixel dominance in standard metrics rewards blob-correct methods over boundary-correct ones, and users overwhelmingly need boundaries.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Region-integral metrics allocate weight proportionally to area, so large-interior correctness dominates scores while boundary fidelity contributes marginally, and downstream applications like editing consume boundaries directly.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method rankings under boundary-localized metrics diverge sharply from area-metric rankings for open-vocabulary systems specifically, because language-driven methods blur boundaries in characteristic ways that area metrics forgive.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Scoring public open-vocabulary methods with boundary-band metrics will change rank order relative to standard mIoU more than it does for supervised methods, indicating a family-specific boundary weakness hidden by current reporting.
why_important: Adopters choosing systems for editing, measurement, or medical delineation are being guided by a metric misaligned with their utility function.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Boundary metrics exist and are occasionally reported; the claim that they specifically rerank the open-vocabulary family relative to supervised systems may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a panel of open-vocabulary and supervised segmenters under standard and boundary-band metrics on shared benchmarks, and compare rank-change magnitudes between the two families.
main_risk: Boundary metrics are sensitive to annotation precision; benchmarks with high-quality boundary annotation must anchor the study.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] mIoU improvements are assumed to translate proportionally into practical mask quality including boundaries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Language-conditioned scoring operates at patch resolution and inherits text-side spatial vagueness, producing systematically softer boundaries than pixel-supervised methods at equal area scores.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three open-vocabulary and three supervised methods, one benchmark, both metric families: compare rank correlations in one evaluation pass.

one_line_idea: Background-region conventions are inconsistent across dense benchmarks and methods, and harmonizing background handling alone shifts reported open-vocabulary gaps enough to change some published conclusions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks differ in whether unlabeled pixels are ignored, scored as a background class, or partially annotated, and open-vocabulary methods differ in whether they can even express a background prediction.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Interaction between per-benchmark background conventions and per-method background capabilities injects systematic score distortions, favoring methods whose failure modes align with each benchmark's convention, and a harmonized protocol changes cross-paper comparisons materially.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-evaluating methods under unified background protocols will move method gaps by amounts comparable to typical claimed improvements, with the direction of movement predictable from each method's background mechanism.
why_important: An invisible protocol degree of freedom that moves scores at the scale of claimed contributions undermines the cumulative interpretability of the literature.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Background handling is discussed in dataset papers; a quantified cross-method audit of convention-times-mechanism interactions may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Catalogue background conventions across benchmarks and mechanisms across methods, define two harmonized protocols, and re-evaluate a method panel under both, reporting gap movements.
main_risk: Harmonization requires modifying some methods' inference to express or suppress background, and those modifications must be minimal and documented to avoid unfairness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Background handling is assumed to be a benchmark detail affecting all methods equally and canceling in comparisons.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Methods differ structurally in background expressiveness, so conventions cannot cancel; they interact with mechanisms to create method-specific biases.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two methods with different background mechanisms, one benchmark, two conventions: check whether the inter-method gap moves across conventions in one day.
