one_line_idea: A query-in-the-wild protocol, evaluating dense models on free-form user queries collected without benchmark vocabulary constraints, would reveal a large gap between benchmark scores and experienced quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark queries are canonical noun phrases from fixed lists, while real users issue underspecified, compositional, and pragmatically loaded queries that no current dense benchmark represents.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model success rates on genuinely free-form queries are far below benchmark scores on the same images, and failures cluster in query types (functional descriptions, pragmatic ellipsis, uncommon granularities) that benchmark vocabularies structurally exclude.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Collecting unconstrained queries from users interacting with images and scoring model outputs by human judgment will show success far below benchmark levels for the same models and images, with a stable taxonomy of unrepresented query types accounting for most failures.
why_important: The benchmark-to-experience gap determines whether the field's metrics predict product quality at all; the failure taxonomy also becomes a roadmap for the next benchmark generation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Wild-query evaluations exist for chatbots; a rigorous free-form-query dense segmentation protocol with failure taxonomy may not have been built.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a small user study collecting free-form segmentation requests on benchmark images, evaluate several models with blinded human judgment, and compare success rates to the same models' benchmark scores.
main_risk: Human judgment of mask correctness for underspecified queries is itself ambiguous; judgment protocols with adjudication and agreement reporting are necessary.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark improvements are assumed to translate monotonically into better user-facing dense capability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmark vocabularies were designed to be answerable, filtering out precisely the query distribution users actually generate, so the two performance measures may barely correlate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty images, five users writing natural requests each, one model, human scoring: a one-week pilot quantifying the gap on a small scale.

one_line_idea: Dense benchmark images overlap VLM pretraining corpora, and contamination-stratified scoring shows open-vocabulary methods earning part of their zero-shot reputation on effectively seen images.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense benchmarks are built from web-sourced images, VLM pretraining scrapes the same web, and dense evaluation does not stratify by pretraining exposure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-image dense performance is measurably higher on benchmark images with close pretraining-corpus matches, and the contaminated fraction contributes disproportionately to headline zero-shot numbers.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matching benchmark images against an open pretraining corpus by near-duplicate retrieval will identify a contaminated subset on which dense scores are systematically higher, and decontaminated scores will be lower with method-dependent drops.
why_important: Zero-shot dense claims underpin adoption decisions; exposure-stratified reporting is the minimum correction if contamination inflates them.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contamination studies target classification and language benchmarks; a dense-prediction contamination audit with per-image exposure stratification may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Index an open pretraining corpus for near-duplicate retrieval, tag one benchmark's images by match strength, and compare dense metrics across exposure strata for several models trained on that corpus.
main_risk: Only models with public pretraining data can be audited directly; conclusions about closed-data models remain extrapolations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Zero-shot dense evaluation is assumed uncontaminated because segmentation labels were never in pretraining, ignoring image-side exposure benefits.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Image exposure alone improves feature quality on those exact images, and dense metrics are sensitive enough to register that advantage even without label leakage.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Near-duplicate retrieval between one benchmark and one open corpus, then a two-strata score comparison for one open-data model, in a couple of days.

one_line_idea: Region-text alignment fine-tuning on detection-vocabulary data narrows the effective open vocabulary while improving benchmarks, and vocabulary-coverage audits before and after would expose the hidden tradeoff.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Open-vocabulary segmenters are commonly fine-tuned with region-text supervision derived from detection datasets whose vocabulary is a tiny structured subset of natural language.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Such fine-tuning re-centers the text-alignment manifold on the supervision vocabulary, improving in-distribution names while measurably degrading dense alignment for names outside the supervision distribution, a tradeoff invisible in standard benchmark suites whose vocabularies resemble the supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Broad-vocabulary probing before and after region-text fine-tuning will show coverage contraction, with the largest dense-accuracy losses on names lexically distant from the supervision vocabulary, even as standard benchmarks improve.
why_important: The community may be optimizing itself into narrow-vocabulary systems while believing benchmarks certify openness, a direction error compounding with every fine-tuned generation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Forgetting is studied per-task; vocabulary-manifold contraction under region-text fine-tuning with distance-stratified analysis may be uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one model with standard region-text data, probe dense alignment on a broad stratified vocabulary before and after, and map accuracy change against lexical distance from supervision names.
main_risk: Broad-vocabulary probing needs dense ground truth for rare names, which is scarce; retrieval-style proxies may be needed with validation on the subset that has labels.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Region-text fine-tuning is presented as strictly improving grounding, with standard benchmark suites accepted as proof of retained openness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gradient pressure concentrates alignment capacity on supervised names, and benchmark vocabularies overlap supervision vocabularies enough to hide the contraction from view.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare one public model against its own fine-tuned variant on a rare-name dense probe set, in one evaluation day.

one_line_idea: Self-training with VLM-generated pseudo-masks amplifies text-side biases round over round: classes favored by text geometry gain pixels each iteration, and the drift is measurable, predictable, and correctable with text-side debiasing.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Pseudo-labeling pipelines use VLM dense predictions as supervision for the next model generation, and those predictions carry systematic class biases from text-embedding geometry.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Iterative self-training compounds text-geometry biases multiplicatively, expanding hub-class pixel share and shrinking crowded-neighborhood classes each round, with drift rate predictable from initial text-side statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Tracking per-class pixel share across self-training rounds will show monotone drift aligned with text-geometry predictions, and applying text-side bias correction before pseudo-label generation will flatten the drift without hurting overall accuracy.
why_important: Self-training is the main path to scaling dense supervision cheaply; uncorrected compounding bias would silently corrupt every model trained this way.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Confirmation bias in self-training is known generically; its text-geometry-specific mechanism and predictability for dense VLM pipelines may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a controlled multi-round self-training loop on one benchmark, log per-class pixel share per round, correlate drift with text-side bias predictors, and A-B test debiased pseudo-labeling.
main_risk: Drift may interact with dataset class imbalance; synthetic rebalancing controls are needed to separate the text-geometry component.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Pseudo-label noise is assumed roughly unbiased, with quality filtering considered sufficient protection for self-training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Filtering by confidence selects exactly the predictions where text-geometry bias is strongest, feeding the bias preferentially into the next generation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two self-training rounds on a subset, per-class pixel-share tracking against text-crowding scores, in a few days of training small heads.

one_line_idea: Caption-supervised grounding learns co-occurrence, not localization: models ground nouns onto co-occurring context regions, and counterfactual scenes where usual context appears without the object expose the difference cleanly.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Weakly supervised dense alignment learns from image-caption pairs where a mentioned object and its typical context are both present, providing no signal to separate the object from its context.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A significant portion of caption-supervised grounding places mass on context regions rather than object regions, quantifiable by context-only counterfactuals, and the co-occurrence share predicts which classes will fail in unusual contexts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On scenes containing typical context without the object, caption-supervised models will assign substantial query mass to context regions, and per-class context-mass will predict accuracy drops on out-of-context object placements.
why_important: Weak supervision is the scaling story for dense alignment; knowing it learns context association rather than object localization changes both training design and reliability expectations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context reliance is known for classifiers; a counterfactual-based decomposition of caption-supervised dense grounding into object and context components may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate context-without-object and object-out-of-context sets for common classes, measure query-mass allocation of caption-supervised models on both, and correlate the two failure measures per class.
main_risk: Context-without-object images may contain subtle object traces; verified-absence curation is essential.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Attention or similarity peaks on correct objects in demo figures are taken as evidence that weak supervision teaches localization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The training signal rewards any region predictive of the caption, and context is often more predictive than the object itself, especially for small objects in characteristic scenes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Thirty context-only images for five classes, one caption-supervised model: measure query-mass on context regions in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: The missing dense alignment in contrastive VLMs is a shallow, learnable transform: a small frozen-backbone decoder trained on limited data recovers most of the gap to full fine-tuning, showing the information was present but misformatted.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Full fine-tuning of VLM backbones for segmentation is expensive and erodes open-vocabulary generality, yet it remains the default because frozen-feature baselines have historically lagged.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dense-task gap between frozen and fine-tuned backbones is mostly attributable to a fixable feature-formatting mismatch (spatial mixing, scale composition, alignment recalibration) learnable by a compact decoder, not to missing information in frozen features.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A carefully designed lightweight decoder over frozen features will close most of the frozen-versus-fine-tuned gap across dense benchmarks at a small fraction of trainable parameters, while preserving open-vocabulary performance that fine-tuning degrades.
why_important: If frozen backbones suffice, dense adaptation becomes cheap, composable, and non-destructive, changing the economics of building dense systems on foundation models.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Frozen-feature segmentation exists; a systematic information-versus-formatting decomposition with open-vocabulary retention accounting may be undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched-capacity decoder variants over frozen and fine-tuned backbones on identical data, measure the residual gap, and jointly report open-vocabulary retention for both paths.
main_risk: Decoder design space is large; a weak decoder would understate frozen-feature potential, so the search must be honest and compute-matched against the fine-tuning baseline.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Full fine-tuning is assumed necessary because frozen features are believed to lack dense-task information.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Probing studies repeatedly find rich spatial information in frozen features that naive heads fail to exploit, suggesting formatting rather than absence explains the gap.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, frozen versus fine-tuned backbone with one strong compact decoder each: gap measurement plus an open-vocabulary retention check in a few days.

one_line_idea: Patch-level contrastive alignment objectives are ill-posed at boundaries because patches straddle classes, and boundary-aware assignment during training removes a systematic soft-boundary artifact that plagues all patch-supervised dense models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense alignment training assigns each patch a single text target even though boundary patches contain multiple classes, forcing the model to learn averaged targets exactly where precision matters most.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Single-target patch supervision at boundaries causes characteristic boundary softening and class bleeding in trained models, and mixture-target or subpatch-weighted objectives eliminate the artifact with measurable boundary-metric gains at no interior cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models trained with boundary-aware targets will show concentrated improvements in boundary-band metrics over single-target training under identical data and compute, and the improvement will scale with the fraction of boundary patches in training data.
why_important: A training-objective artifact that structurally caps boundary quality affects every patch-supervised dense system, and the fix is objective-level, cheap, and general.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label smoothing and soft assignment exist broadly; a boundary-specific diagnosis and targeted objective for patch-text alignment may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models on one dataset with single-target versus mixture-target patch supervision, evaluate boundary and interior metrics separately, and ablate the effect by boundary-patch fraction.
main_risk: Gains may be small at typical patch sizes; the experiment should include a coarse-patch condition where the effect is amplified for detectability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Boundary softness in dense VLM outputs is attributed to feature resolution, with the supervision format assumed innocent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The objective explicitly teaches boundary patches to match blended targets, so the model reproduces exactly the blend it was taught, independent of resolution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Small-scale paired training on one dataset at coarse patch size, boundary-band metric comparison, in a few days on modest compute.

one_line_idea: Fine-tuning the text tower for dense tasks is more damaging to open-vocabulary ability than fine-tuning the vision tower: alignment forgetting is asymmetric across towers, and freezing choice should follow the asymmetry.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense adaptation recipes vary arbitrarily in which towers they unfreeze, and the field lacks a controlled account of how tower choice affects open-vocabulary retention.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Text-tower updates on narrow-vocabulary dense data distort the global text manifold, damaging alignment for all unsupervised names, while vision-tower updates generalize benignly across the visual domain, producing a strong retention asymmetry favoring frozen text towers.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A factorial freeze-unfreeze experiment across towers under identical dense supervision will show unseen-name dense performance degrading far more when the text tower trains, with the effect growing as supervision vocabulary shrinks.
why_important: A validated freezing rule would immediately improve every dense adaptation recipe and explain retention differences among published systems as tower-choice artifacts.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Freezing ablations appear per-paper; a systematic cross-tower retention asymmetry study with vocabulary-size scaling may be absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the four freeze combinations on one model and dataset, evaluate seen-name and unseen-name dense performance, and repeat at two supervision-vocabulary sizes.
main_risk: Asymmetry may depend on relative tower capacities and learning rates; hyperparameter sweeps per condition are needed for a fair comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Tower freezing is treated as an efficiency choice rather than a determinant of open-vocabulary retention.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A narrow supervision vocabulary constrains text-tower gradients to a low-dimensional subspace whose optimization warps the manifold globally, while visual gradients remain anchored by diverse pixel statistics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two conditions (text frozen versus unfrozen, vision trained in both) on one dataset, unseen-name dense evaluation, in a couple of training days.

one_line_idea: Training dense models on synthetic captions transfers the captioner's blind spots as a hard ceiling: student dense performance per concept is bounded by the teacher captioner's mention behavior, creating invisible inherited gaps.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense-alignment pipelines increasingly generate synthetic captions or region descriptions with off-the-shelf captioners to scale supervision, and captioners systematically under-mention certain object types, materials, and states.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Concepts the teacher captioner rarely mentions receive proportionally weak dense alignment in the student regardless of visual prevalence, so teacher mention statistics predict student per-concept dense accuracy, and diversifying teachers measurably lifts the inherited floor.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Student per-concept dense accuracy will correlate strongly with teacher mention frequency computed over the synthetic corpus, and a multi-teacher captioning mix will improve exactly the concepts where single-teacher mention rates were lowest.
why_important: Synthetic supervision is becoming the dominant scaling path; understanding inheritance dynamics prevents building a generation of dense models sharing one captioner's blind spots.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Teacher-student distillation bias is studied for classification; mention-statistics-mediated inheritance for dense alignment may be uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train dense students on single-teacher and multi-teacher synthetic captions over the same images, compute teacher mention statistics, and test the correlation and the multi-teacher recovery effect.
main_risk: Mention frequency correlates with visual prevalence; the analysis must condition on ground-truth prevalence from densely annotated subsets.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic captions are treated as a nearly free supervision multiplier whose quality issues average out at scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scale amplifies rather than averages a single teacher's systematic omissions, since every image passes through the same mention filter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute mention statistics of one popular captioner over a benchmark's images and correlate with a caption-trained model's per-class dense scores, requiring no new training.

one_line_idea: Mixing instance-mask and semantic-mask supervision teaches conflicting notions of object extent, and the conflict measurably hurts referring tasks that need instances, suggesting supervision-type should be conditioned, not pooled.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense training corpora combine datasets annotated with instance masks, semantic regions, and panoptic conventions, pooled under one training objective as if extent semantics agreed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pooled training on conflicting extent conventions produces models with unstable instance-versus-region behavior, harming instance-critical tasks like referring segmentation, and conditioning the model on the intended convention via a task token recovers the loss.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Models trained on pooled conventions will show higher variance in instance separation and worse referring accuracy than convention-conditioned models trained on identical data, with errors concentrated on classes where conventions disagree most.
why_important: Everyone pools segmentation datasets for scale; if pooling degrades instance behavior, a one-token fix recovers performance the field is currently leaving behind.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-dataset training conflicts are discussed for label spaces; extent-convention conflict and its conditioning remedy for language-grounded dense models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models on pooled data with and without convention-conditioning tokens, evaluate instance-critical and region-critical tasks separately, and analyze error concentration by convention-disagreement classes.
main_risk: Convention labels per dataset are coarse; some datasets mix conventions internally, adding noise to the conditioning signal.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More mask data is assumed better regardless of annotation convention, with pooling treated as harmless.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The same visual object receives contradictory extent targets across datasets, an irreducible label conflict under pooling that only conditioning can resolve.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one pooled-trained public model for instance-separation consistency on classes with known convention conflicts versus agreement classes, from released predictions in a day.

one_line_idea: Part queries retrieve wholes: language-grounded segmenters asked for object parts return whole-object masks because caption supervision represents parts as attributes of wholes rather than as spatial units.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Captions mention parts mostly in whole-object contexts, and dense benchmarks focus on objects, so part-level grounding is weakly supervised and rarely evaluated.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Part-query failure follows a specific signature, near-correct object selection with near-total part-boundary failure, indicating that part names are aligned to whole-object regions in feature space, and part-specific evaluation will show this signature across model families.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On part-annotated benchmarks, part-query IoU against part ground truth will be low while overlap of the same predictions with the parent object will be high, confirming whole-retrieval rather than random error, consistently across architectures.
why_important: Part-level grounding is essential for manipulation, repair, and medical applications; the failure signature identifies what supervision is missing rather than just that scores are low.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Part segmentation exists as a supervised task; the whole-retrieval failure-signature analysis for open-vocabulary part queries may be undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Query several open-vocabulary models with part names on a part-annotated benchmark, score against part and parent-object ground truth separately, and compute the signature ratio per model.
main_risk: Part name ambiguity (handle, top) may cause unrelated errors that dilute the signature; polysemy screening of the part vocabulary is needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Part-query failure is assumed to be general open-vocabulary weakness rather than a structured whole-retrieval bias.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Caption co-occurrence binds part names to whole-object visual evidence, so the learned alignment for a part name points at the whole by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten part queries on one part-annotated benchmark with one model: report part-IoU versus parent-object-overlap in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Natural-language granularity cues (the whole X, just the Y of the X) fail to control mask extent reliably, while an explicit granularity token interface succeeds, showing granularity is representable but not language-accessible.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Users need to control whether a query selects an object, its parts, or a group, and current interfaces offer only natural-language phrasing whose effect on mask granularity is undocumented.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense models represent multiple granularities internally, but linguistic granularity cues fail to select among them reliably, so structured granularity conditioning outperforms even carefully engineered phrasings by a wide margin.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Systematic phrasing sweeps will show weak, inconsistent granularity control across models, while models with explicit granularity inputs will show strong control on identical stimuli, and probing will confirm multi-granularity information in shared representations.
why_important: Granularity control is a daily-use requirement for interactive segmentation; knowing language cannot reach an existing capability redirects interface design immediately.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-granularity segmentation exists with point prompts; the language-accessibility gap for granularity selection may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build stimuli with valid object, part, and group targets, sweep granularity phrasings across models, compare against granularity-token systems, and probe frozen features for granularity information.
main_risk: Phrasing sweeps can miss the magic phrase; large systematic phrase sets and prompt-optimization baselines guard against understating language control.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Richer instruction tuning is expected to eventually give language full control over output granularity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Granularity words are among the least visually grounded tokens in captions, so alignment training gives them no consistent dense meaning to control anything with.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten scenes with nested targets, fifteen phrasings, one model: quantify phrasing-to-granularity consistency in a day.

one_line_idea: Predicted part and whole masks violate containment at high rates, and enforcing part-whole consistency at inference is a free accuracy and trustworthiness gain no current system exploits.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Language-grounded segmenters answer part and whole queries independently, with no mechanism enforcing that a part mask lies inside its parent object mask.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Containment violations between independently predicted part and whole masks are frequent, correlate strongly with error in at least one of the two masks, and projecting predictions onto the containment-consistent set improves both masks on average.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring containment violation rates across public models will show substantial violations, violation magnitude will predict mask error, and consistency projection will yield net IoU gains on both part and whole queries without retraining.
why_important: Logical consistency of outputs is both a cheap accuracy source and a prerequisite for downstream systems that reason over scene structure; violations also provide a label-free error signal.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Structured-consistency enforcement is common in supervised hierarchical segmentation; its diagnostic and corrective use for open-vocabulary language-queried models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Query part-whole pairs across a part-annotated benchmark, quantify violations and their correlation with error, and evaluate a projection step that resolves inconsistencies by confidence-weighted adjustment.
main_risk: Some part-whole relations are ambiguous or context-dependent, requiring a vetted relation inventory to avoid enforcing false constraints.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-query independence is treated as harmless, with consistency expected to emerge from model quality rather than be enforced.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Independent decoding of related queries wastes a known logical constraint, and constraint projection mathematically cannot hurt when one mask is reliably better than the other.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty part-whole query pairs, one model: violation rate and post-projection IoU delta in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Open-vocabulary segmenters exhibit basic-level bias: superordinate queries like animal produce worse masks than basic-level names for the same regions, because caption language overwhelmingly uses basic-level terms.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Users query at whatever abstraction level suits their task, and psycholinguistics establishes that captions and everyday language prefer basic-level category names.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense alignment strength varies systematically across abstraction levels with a peak at the basic level, so superordinate and subordinate queries for identical regions yield measurably worse masks, in proportion to each level's caption usage frequency.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Querying the same ground-truth regions at three abstraction levels will show a basic-level peak in IoU across models and categories, with the superordinate penalty larger than the subordinate penalty, matching caption-usage asymmetries.
why_important: Vocabulary-level effects mean system quality depends on the user's abstraction choice, an unmeasured usability hazard, and level-aware query rewriting becomes a free fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Basic-level effects are classic in cognition; their quantitative expression in dense VLM alignment and a rewriting remedy may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build level-triplet vocabularies for benchmark categories, evaluate identical regions under all levels, and test superordinate-to-basic query rewriting as an inference-time fix.
main_risk: Level assignment is category-dependent and sometimes contested; the level inventory needs independent linguistic grounding.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A correct name at any abstraction level is assumed roughly equally usable by open-vocabulary systems.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Alignment strength per name tracks caption exposure, and caption exposure is sharply peaked at the basic level, making the effect near-inevitable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten categories, three levels each, one model on one benchmark: per-level IoU comparison in a day.

one_line_idea: Stuff-stuff boundary placement is learned as dataset convention, not visual inference: models transfer their training dataset's boundary style to new domains, and cross-dataset boundary disagreement quantifies this hidden convention learning.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Boundaries between stuff regions like grass-sidewalk or sky-mountain are annotated with dataset-specific conventions, and open-vocabulary models are evaluated across datasets as if boundary ground truth were convention-free.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models reproduce their dense-training dataset's stuff-boundary conventions on foreign domains, so cross-dataset stuff-boundary error contains a systematic convention component separable from perceptual error, and convention adaptation with tiny calibration data recovers it.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Boundary-band errors on foreign datasets will show systematic directional biases matching training-convention differences, and a few calibration images will recover a large fraction of stuff-boundary error while leaving thing boundaries unchanged.
why_important: Separating convention error from capability error changes how cross-dataset results are read, and the cheap calibration fix improves practical transfer immediately.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Annotation-convention differences are acknowledged qualitatively; their quantitative isolation in boundary transfer and a calibration remedy may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or take models with known dense-training provenance, measure directional boundary biases across dataset pairs for shared stuff-class adjacencies, and evaluate few-shot convention calibration.
main_risk: Shared stuff-class pairs across datasets are limited, constraining statistical power; simulation with re-annotated subsets can supplement.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cross-dataset boundary error is interpreted wholly as model imprecision rather than partly as convention mismatch.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Stuff transitions are genuinely ambiguous, so annotation conventions fill the ambiguity, and any model fitting one convention must contradict another in predictable directions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One shared stuff adjacency across two datasets, one model trained on each: compare directional boundary offsets in a day of analysis.

one_line_idea: Linguistic countability drives segmentation topology: mass-noun phrasing yields merged regions and count-noun phrasing yields instance-like masks for the same visual material, an unmeasured coupling between grammar and mask structure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The same visual content can be queried with mass syntax (water, foliage) or count syntax (a puddle, a bush), and dense systems return masks whose topology users implicitly trust to reflect the scene rather than the grammar.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Mask connectivity and instance structure vary systematically with the query's countability syntax rather than only with visual evidence, revealing that output topology is partly a linguistic artifact, exploitable for control but dangerous when unnoticed.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Paired mass-versus-count queries over identical scenes will produce systematically different component counts and connectivity, consistent across scenes, and the effect will persist when visual content is held fixed and only syntax varies.
why_important: Downstream consumers use mask topology for counting, measuring, and interaction; grammar-driven topology means silent errors in all of them, but also offers a free control channel if characterized.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Countability is a known linguistic dimension; its causal effect on predicted mask topology in dense VLMs may be unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct minimal-pair queries differing only in countability syntax over scenes with ambiguous material-object structure, and quantify topology differences in predicted masks across models.
main_risk: Some paired phrasings shift meaning beyond countability; linguistic validation of minimal pairs is required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mask topology is assumed to be determined by the image, with query phrasing affecting only which concept is selected.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training data pairs mass syntax with region-style masks and count syntax with instance-style masks, teaching the topology-grammar coupling as a statistical regularity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifteen scenes, paired mass and count queries, one model: compare connected-component statistics between conditions in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Ordinal reference (the second cup from the left) grounds at near-chance across dense models because ordinal computation requires an explicit sort the architectures never perform, and errors follow a predictable off-by-adjacency pattern.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Ordinal expressions are routine in natural instructions, and referring benchmarks contain few ordinal samples, leaving the capability unmeasured while interfaces assume it works.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense grounding lacks any mechanism to enumerate and rank candidate instances along an axis, so ordinal accuracy will sit near the chance level given the candidate count, with errors concentrated on adjacent ranks rather than random, indicating partial but insufficient ordering signal.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On controlled ordinal suites with varying instance counts, accuracy will track slightly above one-over-n with adjacent-rank confusions dominating, and no current architecture family will escape the pattern without explicit enumeration scaffolding.
why_important: Ordinal reference is a core disambiguation strategy for humans; near-chance performance means interactive systems will fail on a construction users reach for constantly.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Counting weaknesses are known broadly; a rank-resolved error analysis of ordinal dense grounding with the adjacency signature may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate scenes with aligned instance arrays of varying counts, evaluate ordinal queries across model families, and analyze the rank-confusion structure against chance and adjacency models.
main_risk: Axis ambiguity (whose left) must be controlled with unambiguous viewer-frame layouts to isolate ordinal computation from frame confusion.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Ordinal failures are lumped into general counting weakness, expected to improve automatically with scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ordinal grounding requires a discrete algorithmic operation, sorting by coordinate, that gradient-trained dense matchers have no representational incentive to implement.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Thirty arrayed-instance scenes, ordinal queries at three positions, one model: accuracy versus chance and the adjacency-confusion share in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Instance counts derived from language-grounded segmentation systematically undercount in crowded scenes with a density-dependent bias, and the bias curve is stable enough to invert for calibrated counting.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A natural pipeline for open-vocabulary counting is to segment all instances of a named class and count components, but segmentation models merge adjacent instances under crowding in ways counting benchmarks for this pipeline do not characterize.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Undercounting bias grows smoothly with true instance density and inter-instance overlap, is stable across scene types for a fixed model, and can be estimated once and inverted to produce calibrated counts with quantified uncertainty.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Count-error curves versus density will be monotone and model-specific but stable across domains, and applying the inverted bias curve will substantially reduce counting error on held-out crowded scenes compared to raw component counting.
why_important: Open-vocabulary counting has immediate applications in inventory, ecology, and inspection; a calibrated correction converts a biased pipeline into a usable measurement instrument.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Crowd counting is its own field; characterizing and inverting the density-dependent bias of language-grounded segmentation counting may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate segmentation-based counting across density strata on counting-annotated datasets, fit per-model bias curves, and validate inverted-curve calibration on held-out domains.
main_risk: Bias stability across domains is the load-bearing assumption; if merging behavior is scene-type-dependent, calibration will not transfer and the idea fails informatively.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Segmentation-based counting is assumed either adequate as-is or hopeless under crowding, without a calibration middle path.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instance merging is driven by local geometry statistics that recur across domains, making the bias a function of density more than of content.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One counting dataset with density annotations, one model: fit the bias curve on half, test inversion on the other half, in two days.

one_line_idea: Complement queries (everything except the sky) fail despite being trivially computable from the affirmative mask, exposing that dense systems lack a negation-as-set-operation pathway even where no perception is required.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The complement of a segmentable region is itself a well-defined region requiring zero additional perception, yet language interfaces process except-constructions through the same text-matching pathway as ordinary queries.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense systems fail complement queries at high rates while succeeding on the corresponding affirmative queries, demonstrating that failure is located purely in linguistic-operational parsing, and a lightweight query-rewriting layer that detects set operations and composes affirmative masks fixes it completely.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Paired affirmative-complement evaluation will show large accuracy gaps closed almost entirely by an external parse-and-compose wrapper, across all tested dense models.
why_important: It cleanly separates perceptual capability from operational language handling and shows a class of failures fixable by interface logic rather than model scale, a finding with immediate product value.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Set-operation query handling for dense models seems unbenchmarked, and the diagnosis that these failures are purely operational may be undemonstrated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build paired affirmative and complement queries on standard benchmarks, evaluate models raw and with a set-operation wrapper, and attribute the gap closure.
main_risk: Complement ground truth depends on scene coverage conventions (what counts as everything); protocol definitions must be explicit.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Complement failures are folded into general negation weakness presumed to require better language understanding inside the model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The failure requires no new understanding to fix, only recognizing the construction and applying mask arithmetic, which is why a wrapper should close it entirely.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty affirmative-complement pairs, one model, with and without a hand-written rewrite rule: gap and closure measured in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Attribute-only queries (everything red) are object-mediated: models find red objects but miss red stuff and red object-parts, revealing that attributes are grounded through object nouns rather than as pixel properties.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Color and material attributes are pixel-level properties in principle, but caption supervision presents attributes almost exclusively as noun modifiers, and attribute-only dense queries are absent from standard benchmarks.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense responses to bare-attribute queries will cover attribute-bearing objects while systematically missing attribute-bearing stuff regions and parts, with the miss rate predicting a general principle that dense grounding routes through object-noun representations.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Recall of bare-attribute queries will be far higher on pixels inside nameable objects than on equally attribute-positive stuff pixels, across attributes and models, and appending generic nouns (red things) will not close the stuff gap.
why_important: Attribute-level selection is a natural editing and search primitive; knowing it is object-mediated predicts precise failure classes and motivates pixel-property probing objectives.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attribute grounding is studied with object contexts; the object-versus-stuff recall asymmetry for bare-attribute dense queries may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct attribute ground truth over objects and stuff via color-calibrated annotation on benchmark images, evaluate bare-attribute queries, and compare recall across pixel classes.
main_risk: Attribute ground truth for stuff requires careful perceptual annotation standards, since color naming over textures is itself variable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Color queries are assumed to be the easy case for vision-language systems since color is low-level and abundant in captions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every caption occurrence of red modifies a noun, so the learned alignment for red is a direction within object representations, not a pixel-property detector.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten images with red objects and red stuff regions, bare-attribute query, one model: object-versus-stuff recall comparison in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Comparative attribute grounding (the darker of the two) is near chance because per-pixel scoring has no cross-instance normalization step, and adding an explicit candidate-comparison stage fixes it without touching the backbone.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Comparative constructions require evaluating a property across candidate instances and selecting by relative rank, while dense pipelines score each pixel or region independently against the query text.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Independent-scoring architectures cannot represent relative comparisons, so comparative-query accuracy will hover near random selection among candidates, and a lightweight external stage that extracts per-candidate property values and compares them will restore high accuracy using the same backbone.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparative-query accuracy will be near one-over-candidates for standard pipelines regardless of scale, and the external comparison stage will lift it dramatically, demonstrating the failure is architectural rather than representational.
why_important: Comparatives are among the most efficient disambiguation devices in language; an architecture-level diagnosis with a modular fix advances both understanding and practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Comparative grounding failures are noted anecdotally; the independent-scoring diagnosis with a modular restoration experiment may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build two-candidate comparative suites across several attributes, evaluate standard pipelines and the same pipelines with an external compare-then-select stage, and measure the restoration effect.
main_risk: The external stage needs reliable per-candidate property extraction, whose own errors must be accounted for in attributing the fix.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Comparative failures are expected to resolve with stronger language models attached to the vision system.
why_it_might_be_wrong: No amount of language strength helps if the scoring interface never sees both candidates jointly; the computation is missing, not weak.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty two-candidate scenes, one attribute, one pipeline with and without a trivial brightness-comparison wrapper: accuracy delta in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Dense systems treat conjunctive and disjunctive queries identically: cats and dogs versus cats or dogs produce indistinguishable masks, revealing that logical connectives are dropped at the grounding interface.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Logical connectives change query semantics decisively in set terms, and no standard dense benchmark evaluates connective sensitivity.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Predicted masks for conjunction and disjunction over the same class pair will be statistically indistinguishable across current systems, because text encoders compress both to similar embeddings and mask decoders have no set-semantics pathway.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Mask-difference statistics between connective variants will be within noise across models, while human-expected differences are categorical; text-embedding distances between the variants will be tiny, localizing the information loss to the text side.
why_important: Connectives are basic instruction vocabulary; verified insensitivity defines a crisp, teachable failure class and motivates set-aware query compilation for practical systems.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Connective insensitivity is documented for retrieval ranking; its dense-output verification and text-side localization may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate paired connective queries over class pairs with distinct ground-truth sets, quantify mask differences and text-embedding differences, and compare against a query-compilation baseline that applies mask union or intersection explicitly.
main_risk: Natural conjunction sometimes means joint presence rather than union in human usage; instruction contexts must disambiguate the intended set semantics.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Instruction-tuned grounding systems are assumed to inherit basic logical operator handling from their language components.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The grounding step reduces queries to embedding similarity, where near-synonymous surface forms collapse and set semantics has no representation to survive in.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten class pairs, both connectives, one model: distribution of mask differences versus the explicit union baseline in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Metric-quantitative spatial queries (objects larger than half the image, within ten pixels of the border) are wholly ungrounded in dense systems, and their failure profile shows quantities are parsed as vague intensifiers.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Programmatic use of dense models invites quantitative filters expressed in language, and nothing in contrastive or instruction-tuned training grounds numeric magnitudes to pixel measurements.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense responses to metrically quantified queries will be insensitive to the numeric value, behaving identically across substituted magnitudes, indicating numbers are processed as generic emphasis rather than as measurable constraints.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping the numeric parameter across an order of magnitude will leave predicted masks essentially unchanged for current systems, while a tool-augmented baseline that extracts measurements and filters explicitly will track the parameter faithfully.
why_important: Quantitative language is where perception meets specification; documenting its complete failure defines the boundary between what to ask models and what to compute classically.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Numeric insensitivity is known for text-to-image generation; a parametric-sweep audit for dense grounding may be unperformed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct parametric query families with ground truth computable from annotations, sweep numeric values, and measure response sensitivity across models against the tool-augmented control.
main_risk: Some phrasings may fail for parsing rather than grounding reasons; multiple surface forms per parameter value separate the two.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Instruction-tuned multimodal systems are assumed to handle simple quantitative constraints as part of general instruction following.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Grounding numbers to pixel measurements requires an internal measurement operation that no training signal ever demanded, so the capability has no reason to exist.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One query family at five parameter values, one model: mask-change curve versus parameter, in a few hours.

one_line_idea: State-conditioned queries (the open door, the empty cup) lag object queries by a wide margin at dense level, and the gap measures a state-grounding deficit distinct from object recognition that paired-state scenes isolate cleanly.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Object states are transient properties weakly represented in captions relative to object identities, and dense benchmarks conflate state and identity by rarely including same-object different-state contrasts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense grounding accuracy conditioned on state words will be dramatically lower than on identity words in scenes containing both state alternatives, and the deficit will be text-side dominated, with state words moving text embeddings insufficiently to reorder region scores.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On paired-state scenes with two instances differing only in state, models will select by identity salience near chance with respect to state, and text-embedding displacement from state words will predict the per-model deficit.
why_important: States determine affordances; embodied and assistive applications need state-conditioned grounding more than one more point of object mIoU, yet the capability is unmeasured.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] State recognition exists as a classification task; the dense paired-state audit with text-side attribution may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate paired-state scenes for common state contrasts, evaluate state-conditioned referring across models, and correlate deficits with text-side displacement measurements.
main_risk: Paired-state scenes are scarcer in natural imagery; some staging or synthesis may be needed with realism checks.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] State understanding is assumed to ride along with general vision-language capability improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Captions mention states rarely and inconsistently, so alignment for state words is orders of magnitude weaker than for object names, a gap scale alone will not close.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifteen paired-state scenes, one state contrast, one model: state-conditional selection accuracy in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Segmentation tokens in multimodal LLMs are a low-bandwidth bottleneck: mask fidelity saturates with the information capacity of the token embedding, measurable by comparing token-decoded masks against directly decoded masks from the same visual features.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A prominent architecture family makes multimodal LLMs emit special tokens whose embeddings condition a mask decoder, compressing whatever the language model knows about the target region into one or few vectors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The token-embedding channel is the binding constraint on mask quality: complex, multi-part, or high-detail regions exceed its capacity, and fidelity ceilings will track token count and dimensionality rather than backbone strength.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Mask quality will degrade with target-region complexity faster for token-bottlenecked decoders than for dense-feature decoders on the same backbone, and increasing segmentation-token count will lift the ceiling in proportion, isolating capacity as the mechanism.
why_important: This architecture family is becoming the default dense interface for multimodal LLMs; knowing its scaling bottleneck redirects design toward richer mask-conditioning channels before the pattern ossifies.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The token interface is widely used but its information-capacity analysis as a function of region complexity may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models varying segmentation-token count and dimensionality, evaluate mask quality stratified by region complexity measures, and compare against a dense-conditioning ablation.
main_risk: Region complexity must be quantified carefully (boundary length, component count, genus), and complexity correlates with rarity in training data, requiring stratified sampling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mask errors from these systems are attributed to grounding or reasoning failures of the language model rather than to the conditioning channel's capacity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A single embedding cannot encode arbitrarily detailed spatial layouts as a matter of information theory, so complexity-dependent saturation is forced once regions exceed channel capacity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One public token-based segmenter: stratify its benchmark performance by boundary-length percentiles and check for the predicted complexity-dependent degradation, from released predictions in a day.

one_line_idea: Autoregressive coordinate emission for dense outputs accumulates spatial error along the sequence: later polygon vertices and later boxes in a list are systematically less accurate, an interface artifact invisible to aggregate metrics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Some multimodal LLMs express regions as text-serialized coordinates, generated token by token under autoregressive decoding with each output conditioned on previous outputs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Spatial accuracy decays with sequence position within a single structured output, because early errors condition later predictions and attention to visual evidence dilutes as text context grows, producing a measurable within-output error gradient.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-vertex error will increase with vertex index controlling for geometric difficulty, the effect will strengthen with polygon length, and re-prompting for the same region with reversed serialization order will mirror the gradient, confirming it is positional rather than geometric.
why_important: Serialization order is a free design choice; if it drives an error gradient, simple reordering, chunking, or parallel decoding interventions yield immediate dense-accuracy gains.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Exposure bias is classic for text; its quantitative spatial expression within dense structured outputs of multimodal LLMs may be uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate coordinate-emitting models on polygon tasks, regress per-vertex error on position with geometric covariates, and run the reversed-order control.
main_risk: Vertex correspondence between prediction and ground truth requires careful matching to avoid positional artifacts from the matching algorithm itself.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Coordinate serialization is treated as a lossless output format whose only cost is token budget.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Autoregressive conditioning mathematically propagates early deviations, and no mechanism re-anchors later coordinates to pixels once the text prefix dominates the context.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one polygon benchmark, per-vertex error versus index plus the reversed-order control, in one to two days.

one_line_idea: Chain-of-thought reasoning before mask emission can hurt grounding: reasoning tokens displace visual attention, and mask accuracy on perceptually easy targets drops when models are made to think longer.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Reasoning-before-answering is being adopted for segmentation-capable multimodal LLMs on the assumption that more deliberation monotonically helps.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For perceptually direct targets, long reasoning traces interpose text context that dilutes attention to visual tokens at mask-decoding time, creating a reasoning tax measurable as accuracy loss that grows with trace length on easy cases while possibly helping hard relational cases.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Manipulating reasoning length via prompting on fixed inputs will show a crossover: easy-target accuracy declining with trace length while relationally hard targets improve or plateau, with attention-mass measurements to visual tokens mediating the effect.
why_important: Deliberation policies are being set now for dense multimodal systems; knowing when thinking hurts enables difficulty-adaptive reasoning rather than uniform verbosity.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Reasoning-length effects are studied for text tasks; the visual-attention-dilution mechanism for dense outputs may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one segmentation-capable model under short, medium, and long forced reasoning on difficulty-stratified targets, logging attention mass to visual tokens, and test the crossover and mediation.
main_risk: Forced reasoning length changes more than length (content quality, distraction); multiple prompting strategies per length control for content effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More reasoning is assumed monotonically beneficial or neutral for all multimodal outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask decoding consumes a context window where visual tokens compete with generated text, and every reasoning token mechanically reduces the visual share of attention.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifty easy referring targets, three reasoning-length conditions, one model: accuracy versus length curve in a day.

one_line_idea: Multimodal LLMs are dense-inconsistent across query formats: pointing at a pixel and asking what it is contradicts asking where a named thing is, and cross-format agreement is a label-free quality audit plus a constraint for free improvement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The same underlying dense knowledge can be queried as pixel-to-name (what is here) or name-to-pixels (where is this), and systems are evaluated on each format separately, never on their mutual consistency.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-format contradictions are frequent and concentrate where the model is wrong in at least one format, so agreement serves as an unsupervised correctness signal, and decoding constrained to cross-format consistency improves both formats without retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Contradiction rates will be substantial across current models, agreement will predict correctness with strong discrimination, and consistency-constrained inference will yield net gains on both query formats on standard benchmarks.
why_important: Label-free reliability signals and training-free accuracy gains are rare commodities; consistency auditing also gives deployers a monitoring tool requiring no ground truth.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Round-trip consistency is used in translation and depth estimation; its formulation and exploitation for multimodal dense interfaces may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample pixels and names on benchmark images, query both directions, quantify contradiction structure and its correlation with correctness, then evaluate a consistency-projected decoding scheme.
main_risk: The two formats may share failure modes, making agreement less informative than hoped; the discrimination analysis directly measures this.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-format accuracy is treated as the complete characterization of dense capability, with internal coherence assumed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The two formats exercise different decoding pathways over the same features, and nothing in training ties their outputs together, so incoherence is the default expectation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, fifty images, both query directions on sampled points and names: contradiction rate and its correlation with errors in a day.

one_line_idea: Segmentation-capable multimodal LLMs cannot express spatial uncertainty: their verbalized doubts about mask regions are uncorrelated with actual boundary errors, leaving dense outputs without any usable confidence channel.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Mask decoders in multimodal LLM systems emit hard masks, and the only uncertainty mechanism available is the language channel, whose spatial reliability has not been measured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Elicited verbal uncertainty about specific mask regions (which side is uncertain, where the boundary might err) will show near-zero correspondence with measured error maps, because no training signal ever connected verbal hedging to spatial error statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Region-level correlation between verbalized uncertainty and true error will be negligible across models and elicitation styles, while a simple ensemble-disagreement baseline over the same models will correlate strongly, demonstrating the information exists but the verbal channel cannot carry it.
why_important: Dense outputs feed automated pipelines that need to know where masks may be wrong; documenting the absence of a working confidence channel defines a concrete requirement for the next interface generation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Verbalized-confidence studies exist for question answering; spatially resolved verbal-uncertainty validation for dense outputs may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Elicit structured spatial-uncertainty reports alongside masks, compute region-level error correspondence against ground truth, and compare with sampling-based disagreement over the same models.
main_risk: Elicitation format strongly shapes verbal reports; several formats must be tested before concluding the channel is broken rather than the prompt.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Language models that hedge well on factual questions are assumed able to hedge meaningfully about their spatial outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Verbal hedging was learned from text corpora with no spatial-error feedback loop, so it generalizes to dense outputs only by accident if at all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifty masks with elicited per-side uncertainty ratings, one model: correlation with per-side boundary error in a day.

one_line_idea: Multi-turn mask correction fails because dialog context does not effectively carry mask state: models treat each correction as a fresh query, and correction success barely exceeds single-turn retry rates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Interactive refinement (no, the other one; include the handle too) is the advertised advantage of conversational segmentation interfaces, yet evaluation is almost entirely single-turn.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Current systems lack a functional representation of their previous mask in dialog state, so corrections referencing prior output (the other one, slightly larger) perform no better than independently re-prompting, and explicit mask-state re-injection into context recovers genuine interactive gains.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Correction-turn success will match independent-retry baselines within noise for current systems, while architectures or wrappers that re-encode the previous mask as visual input will show clear above-retry improvements on the same correction suite.
why_important: Interactivity is the main claimed advantage of language-based segmentation over point-and-click tools; if corrections do not actually use dialog state, the advantage is currently fictional and the fix is identifiable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-turn dense correction benchmarks and the retry-baseline comparison establishing whether state is used may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a correction dialog suite with typed correction categories, evaluate systems on correction turns against matched independent-retry baselines, and test mask re-injection wrappers.
main_risk: Correction utterances leak target information that helps even stateless retries; the suite must include corrections interpretable only relative to prior output.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Conversational segmentation systems are assumed to leverage dialog history because their language backbone handles multi-turn text competently.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The previous mask exists as decoder output, not as tokens in context, so the language backbone literally cannot see what it produced and corrections have no referent.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Thirty correction dialogs of the-other-one type, one system: correction success versus independent-retry success in a day.

one_line_idea: Visual prompt overlays (marks, boxes, highlights drawn on the image) contaminate the visual stream: they alter dense predictions for unmarked objects, an interference effect that mark-based prompting studies never control.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Overlay-based visual prompting is popular for directing multimodal model attention, and the overlay physically edits the pixels every downstream computation consumes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Overlays cause measurable prediction changes on regions distant from the mark, including segmentation and labeling flips for unmarked objects, with interference growing with overlay salience and proximity, making mark-based results systematically unclean measurements of the intended question.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing dense outputs on clean versus marked images for queries about unmarked objects will show flip rates well above pixel-noise controls, structured around overlay locations, and overlay styles will trade prompting efficacy against interference along a measurable frontier.
why_important: Overlay prompting is entering evaluation protocols and data-generation pipelines; uncontrolled interference contaminates both, and characterizing the efficacy-interference frontier enables clean protocol design.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mark-based prompting is studied for what it enables; its side effects on unrelated dense predictions may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired clean-marked image sets with queries targeting unmarked content, quantify prediction flips against noise-matched controls, and map interference across overlay styles and distances.
main_risk: Interference may vary strongly by model family and training exposure to synthetic markings, requiring broad model coverage before general claims.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Overlays are treated as transparent communication channels to the model, changing what it attends to but not what it sees.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The overlay is physically part of the image; features are global functions of pixels, so distant contamination is the default and independence would be the surprise.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Thirty images with and without a standard red-circle mark, dense queries on unmarked objects, one model: flip-rate measurement in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: High-resolution tiling strategies for multimodal LLMs improve text-reading tasks far more than segmentation because cross-tile attention fails to reintegrate object geometry, producing task-dependent resolution scaling that current unified benchmarks average away.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal LLMs handle high resolution by encoding image tiles separately plus a low-resolution global view, and resolution improvements are reported as aggregate benchmark gains.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Tiling benefits capabilities that are tile-local (reading, texture, small-object identity) while leaving tile-spanning capabilities (object extent, boundary continuity, part-whole geometry) largely unimproved, because integration across tile boundaries is mediated only by weak global-view features, and task-decomposed scaling curves will reveal this dissociation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Scaling resolution via more tiles will show steep gains on text-reading and small-object naming but flat or marginal gains on segmentation boundary quality for objects spanning tiles, with object-level metrics stratified by tile-spanning status confirming the mechanism.
why_important: Resolution scaling is a major compute expenditure; knowing which capabilities it buys prevents misallocating inference budgets and motivates architectures with genuine cross-tile spatial integration for dense tasks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Tiling architectures are widely deployed; capability-decomposed resolution scaling curves with tile-spanning stratification may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one tiling-based model family across tile-count settings on reading, naming, and segmentation tasks, stratifying dense metrics by whether targets span tile boundaries.
main_risk: Tile-count changes often co-vary with token budgets and training recipes across released checkpoints; controlled inference-time tiling sweeps on one checkpoint are the cleanest design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher input resolution is assumed to improve all fine-grained capabilities of multimodal models roughly uniformly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tile encoders never exchange information at full resolution, so any capability requiring precise cross-tile geometry is structurally excluded from resolution benefits regardless of tile count.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One checkpoint, three tiling settings, one reading task and one segmentation task with tile-spanning stratification: compare the two scaling slopes in two days.
